comments.author: lcarva
comments.body:
> By producing multiple attestations for a single image, do you mean multiple signatures (in the simplesigning attestation format) for a single image?

You quoted the bit about attestation, not signature. Not exactly sure what you mean. Currently, there are three sets of images involved. My terminology could be off, so let me state how I understand things for the sake of clarity:

1. Built Images: the images produced by the task.
2. Signature Images: images that hold a signature for a given built image. These are tagged as `sha256-xxx.sig`.
3. Attestation Images: images that hold one or more attestations for a given built image. Each attestation is a layer in the image. These are tagged as `sha256-xxx.att`.

What the "Multiple Attestations" section is trying to note is that there will likely be multiple layers for Attestation Images once this TEP is implemented. This is because Chains will first create the Attestation Image with a single layer containing the TaskRun attestation, then Chains will add a new layer to the Attestation Image containing the PipelineRun attestation.

I mention that this is not a new behavior because I could have two Tasks that produce type hinting results (e.g. `IMAGE_URL` and `IMAGE_DIGEST`). In that case, even without this TEP, the Attestation Image will contain two layers, each containing a different TaskRun attestation.

> IIUC, currently when Chains extracts image artifacts, it only [looks into the type hinting results at taskrun level](https://github.com/tektoncd/chains/blob/d4b02fef4a10634db20640930e7a46f68eedb389/pkg/artifacts/signable.go#L89-L127). If pipeline level also has the IMAGE_URL and IMAGE_DIGEST results, there will be no another simplesigning attestation generated for the image from pipeline level. Sorry if I misunderstand this.

This TEP makes Chains aware of type hinting on PipelineRun results.

comments.author: Copilot
comments.body: `DefaultResyncPeriod` is set to 10 minutes, which will trigger periodic informer resyncs. Because `LogEventHandlers` logs on Update, this can generate recurring "Namespace config updated" log spam and unnecessary relists even when ConfigMaps are unchanged. Consider disabling resync (0) unless you have a concrete need for periodic reprocessing.

comments.author: Copilot
comments.body: `admissionRequestNamespaceFromContext` reads and then replaces `req.Body` without closing the original body. In a real HTTP server this can prevent the server from closing the original body (since it closes the current `req.Body` at the end), potentially leaking resources. Capture and close the original body after `ReadAll` and before replacing it with the restored reader.

comments.author: Copilot
comments.body: This block re-applies `WithNamespaceConfig` during defaulting. In the admission path, the webhook’s context hook already calls `WithNamespaceConfig`, so this causes duplicate merge work and duplicate info/warn logs for every TaskRun admission request. It’s also easy to accidentally introduce non-idempotent behavior if the merge/parse logic changes. Prefer applying namespace overrides once in the admission/reconciler context hooks and keep `SetDefaults` focused on object defaulting.

comments.author: Copilot
comments.body: As with TaskRun, this re-applies `WithNamespaceConfig` inside `SetDefaults`. The admission controller already merges namespace config into the context before calling defaulting/validation, so this results in duplicate merge work and duplicate logs on every PipelineRun admission request. Consider applying namespace overrides only in the admission/reconciler context hooks.

comments.author: chitrangpatel
comments.body:
I think this was a worry before we implemented the POC @jerop. 

This is what happens currently:

The sidecar runs a script that periodically(every second) executes the following logic:
1. Look for new files (aka. result names) in the directory `/tekton/results`.
2. It keeps a tally of which result (a file in the above directory) it has already checked. This way, each result is only checked once.
3. When a new result is found, it prints it to stdout in a parsable fashion.
4. When all the expected results are looked at, it breaks out of the periodic loop and exits.

On the controller side, every time the reconcile loop runs, the task run controller does the following:
1. Look at the logs of the `results-sidecar` in the task pod.
2. Parse the logs (instead of the termination message) and convert them to results.
3. Attach the results to the task run status.
There is no wait time, it executes with the controller loop.

comments.author: chitrangpatel
comments.body:
The sidecar runs a script that periodically(every second) executes the following logic:

1. Look for new files (aka. result names) in the directory /tekton/results.
2. It keeps a tally of which result (a file in the above directory) it has already checked. This way, each result is only checked once.
3. When a new result is found, it prints it to stdout in a parsable fashion.
4. When all the expected results are looked at, it breaks out of the periodic loop and exits.

Because of this flow, if the sidecar happens to find a file with missing or partial contents, it will think it has already read the results and not re-read it the next time. 

There is a way to get around this by computing the hash of the file contents and ensuring that there is content in the files and when the contents stop changing after a few 1-s loops, we can assume that the results have been written completely. This might add a slight delay but should be safer.

comments.body:
One more alternative here would be to repurpose the Artifact Storage API that Tekton Pipelines already has in place for `PipelineResources`. It already supports buckets and temporary pvcs, and only requires a one-time configuration by operators, no workspaces involved. It transparently moves data between tasks in a pipeline. It's tailored quite closely to the notion of "OutputResources" and "InputResources" but I don't think there's a specific reason that it needs to stay that way.

Docs on setting up storage: https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/main/docs/install.md#configuring-pipelineresource-storage
Here's the interface: https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/main/pkg/artifacts/artifacts_storage.go#L39-L47

> Note that "big" file could be represented as a result too, using a "uniquely identifiable hash" of it, and linking to it for example. Automating this somehow would be nice – something that could hash the content and "capture" some sort of link to where to get the data later and verify it would be super nice.

Depending on which way we go with TEP-0060 we could use this there as well. [Mentioned in that tep briefly](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/pull/547/files#diff-5aec90b863359ee289524e8d80aa7c9b22f80d796b22e740691105de994b606fR387-R394).

Some care needs to be taken as log reading and writing can have races, but this approach is practical and does not mandate granting workloads access to either the API service or some other cluster service.

comments.body: I'm not totally clear on this one - given the use case is supporting UIs/CLIs that report this information it seems like this is a necessary requirement? - Is there a specific use-case in mind for it? Given the non-goal of storing detailed record information I wonder if this is needed.

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body: Yeah I definitely agree - the question is how do we enforce this, given that we don't have a clear mapping between Result data and Record data - Record data is an opaque blob as far as the Results API is concerned. I suspect we might need to introduce similar fields into the Records themselves, so that we can rely on clients to populate the fields, and the Results API can just ensure that these are passed through transparently.

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
> Is there a specific use-case in mind for it? Given the non-goal of storing detailed record information I wonder if this is needed.

The initial idea here is a catch-all for other high level data users might want to aggregate Results by but we don't have a dedicated field for. e.g. things like what repo / project does this Result belong to and other identifying information. I think the intention is to keep this to small key/value pairs to let clients have flexibility while we figure out what other fields we might want to represent directly.

> Who / how does data get recorded into this map? Is it configurable in some way or does the operator need to write code to record to it? Or something else?

Purposefully being agnostic here so client defined, likely by the Result watcher.

The Result API is agnostic to the underlying data, so if a client wanted to do something like store multiple TaskRuns in a single Result (e.g. retries, related runs, etc), we wouldn't stop them. The question there is should we allow multiple summary roots to support that flexibility, or enforce only 1 for simplicity.

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
Not necessarily. The idea is to provide some standardized fields that are common regardless of the underlying record type (with the exception of `annotations`, which is the catch-all generic/opaque map you describe).

One approach is to keep them separate and rely on clients to populate. This makes things like transforming values easier e.g. if we want to convert PipelineRun/TaskRun error reasons to a common error type.

The other option is to have a reference to fields within the Record, (e.g. similar to [additionalPrinterColumns](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/1ecb48215f4dd07bdf2567b5e7c8f7e4939da13b/config/300-pipelinerun.yaml#L73-L85), but this adds complexity to Result retrieval (e.g. for every Result fetch you need to also fetch the Result summary Record).

comments.author: lumjjb
comments.body:
Hi! Sorry about being late to reply. COVID happened :|

Wanted to share a bit more about the thought process around the mocking,

---
### For unit testing

I think the client mocking will work perfectly with unit tests.

----

### For integration

We explored several different approaches when trying to mock SPIRE, a lot of the difficulty in doing so was that test that use mocked SPIRE resulted in two separate processes interacting with the shared state for integration tests. Mocking the workload API for a single memory process is ok, but when two processes (in this case the entrypointer and the controller) need to be able to retrieve compatible crypto material, is where things get a bit messy since we need to maintain state across processes and isolated containers. We would have to mock a daemon server, which pretty much re-implements a bundled version of SPIRE.

The workaround was performing mocking at a slightly higher layer, which takes away the need to have shared state between 2 processes with a fixed seed which would result in the need of an external daemon.

I think there's a desire to have the mocked SPIRE daemon with compatible fake workload client, but it is something that will be at least a couple months work of a dedicated developer.

Another possibility here could also be to create determinism within the ecdsa/rsa crypto library, it's not something I've explored too much.

---

What are some thoughts here? Maybe client mocking for unit tests but keep the higher level mocking for now for the integration/e2e tests - until the SPIRE community makes more progress on a mock server?

comments.author: bobcatfish
comments.body:
To be clear setting the alpha flag should enable the ability to _use_ all alpha features but not necessarily configure them and turn them on. I think there are two things getting mixed together here:
1. Features have stability levels associated with them (alpha/beta/stable) and we are letting operators opt into making these features available via the EnableAPIFields flag
2. Some features are optional (regardless of their stability level), including using SPIRE

SPIRE support will initially be alpha, so the EnableAPIFields should be required to be configured at alpha in order for the SPIRE functionality to be available. However there should still be more configuration required (EnforceNonfalsifiability = SPIRE) in order to turn it on

> Changing the contract that setting alpha flag will enable all alpha features

Hopefully this shouldn't be a change in the contract and should match the description of the alpha feature flag in [TEP-0033](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/blob/main/teps/0033-tekton-feature-gates.md) (or maybe TEP-0033 needs to be updated with more details about a case like this where a feature is alpha but also needs to be opted into? on the other hand it seems like the trend is toward per-feature flags in the future based on some recent discussions)

> Enable SPIRE only if alpha is set and EnforceNonfalsifiability is set to spire.

+1

> Even if the EnforceNonfalsifiability flag is set to spire, if alpha is not enabled then do not enable spire.

Yes this makes sense to me - this could even be treated as an error

comments.author: lumjjb
comments.body:
Yup, exactly! The SPIFFE api doesn't actually have a signing interface where it takes a payload via CSR or likewise. It just provides the identity key material used for the workload to identify itself. The SPIRE Server (+CA) acts as an authority that provides a short term certificate (+key), and says that you can trust this because I've authenticated the workload - parallel to the interaction between fulcio and the OIDC flow of a user.

(The alternative is via JWT signing - more in the other comment below)

comments.author: lumjjb
comments.body:
>im a bit surprised that SPIRE sends the private key to the caller - is there anything that limits how this private key is used after it has been fetched?

Unfortunately no. It is a private key specific to that workload (each pod has its own private key). The implication of this is that there still needs to be controls around preventing service owners from exec'ing (or cgroup hopping) into containers and extracting them (either via filesystem or memory). 

In terms of threat model:
- SPIRE out of the box (assuming secure SPIRE server**) --> can't exfiltrate/impersonate directly through k8s API (excluding exec'ing into containers)
- Using SPIFFE API directly via library (which I think is what we would do) --> private key stays in memory of the cgroup of the process
- Enabling kernel protections against observing memory (i.e. via /proc) --> only susceptible to kernel attacks + hardware observation

**SPIRE server security in the architecture is very important. This is a detail that would influence the threat model. However, it is something independent to the main scope of the TEP that we can address separately as a progressive step too. (The [SPIFFE book](https://spiffe.io/book) chapter: "SPIFFE/SPIRE Applied Concepts
Threat Model", describes this in a bit more detail if interested)

>tekton tasks are executed as pods, which in this proposal would have the SPIRE socket mounted into them - it sounds like a user could add steps into their Task (and resulting pod) that could fetch this private key and upload it somewhere else for use later - am i understanding correctly?

Yes and no, depending on how we end up implementing the SPIFFE interaction. 

Disclaimer: I'm not super familiar with tekton implementation details, so this may be an approximation. 

If the signing responsibility can be done as a sidecar or a step after user controlled input, the SPIRE socket can be made only accessible to those components. As long as it is within the context of the pod.

comments.author: lumjjb
comments.body:
>how does the entrypointer provide the signature and cert? (how large are they, are they small enough to be transmitted via the termination message, and how much space will that leave for the results themselves)

It is done via termination message now. The size of the cert is about 800 bytes, and the size of the signatures is about 100 bytes * (number of fields + 1).

>why does the entrypointer provide the cert - i would have thought the tekton controller would want to request the cert from SPIRE independently, so it knows it can trust it?

The certificate is not used to verify the signature in isolation. It is used to establish the chain of trust from the SPIRE authority to the temporary key used to sign it. 

As you eluded to, the tekton controller (verifier) independently talks to the SPIRE server to obtain the trust bundle, which is used to authenticate the certificate provided. The certificate is used to link the chain of trust, but also used to verify that the one who signed it belongs to the correct pod identity. For example, I should not be able to copy the result of 1 pod's signed results to another.

comments.author: lumjjb

Absolutely. However, the private key is only used to sign outputs of that particular step. So the most it could do is spoof its own results, which could be easily done by specifying the output properly. So there's not too much to gain here since they already have execution control.

I elaborate on this in the other comment about why the cert is part of the output. The check is done to make sure that the signature is for this particular step, so one is not able to sign on behalf of others.

comments.author: lumjjb
comments.body:
Yea most definitely! So let me talk through a bit about the plugin system of SPIRE server then talk about the architecture.

The SPIRE server has a plugin system where it can call out to certain services for certain functions. One of these functions is the upstream CA where all identities would be a part of - the root authority. The plugin system allows the SPIRE server to be configured to talk to existing CA services. I've listed the ones supported below. 

There will definitely be operational cost if the SPIRE server wants to be operated out of cluster. It is mainly a matter of threat model. It isn't really essential in our case to use an upstream CA, because we are using it more as ephermeral keys for signing (the cost may outweigh the risk) - whereas most SPIRE deployments are about end to end authorization of an organization's entire fleet. 

The base requirements of a production deployment of SPIRE would be at least an SQL database (by default it uses local storage if not configured). The CA can then be on disk or as another service. Here are some CA plugins that are supported today.

plugin | name | desc
-- | -- | --
UpstreamAuthority | disk | Uses a CA loaded from disk to sign SPIRE server intermediate certificates.
UpstreamAuthority | aws_pca | Uses a Private Certificate Authority from AWS Certificate Manager to sign SPIRE server intermediate certificates.
UpstreamAuthority | awssecret | Uses a CA loaded from AWS SecretsManager to sign SPIRE server intermediate certificates.
UpstreamAuthority | gcp_cas | Uses a Private Certificate Authority from GCP Certificate Authority Service to sign SPIRE Server intermediate certificates.
UpstreamAuthority | vault | Uses a PKI Secret Engine from HashiCorp Vault to sign SPIRE server intermediate certificates.
UpstreamAuthority | spire | Uses an upstream SPIRE server in the same trust domain to obtain intermediate signing certificates for SPIRE server.
UpstreamAuthority | cert-manager | Uses a referenced cert-manager Issuer to request intermediate signing certificates.

comments.author: lumjjb
comments.body:
>^^ does this sound accurate? i.e. even if you copy the private key (and cert) and make them publicly available, nothing interesting can be done with them outside of the pod that SPIRE has associated them with?

Yes - exactly. It would not verify since the certificate for the fake taskrun would not match up with the details of the task run that is being verified by the controller!

> im still trying to understand if the cert is required - it seems to me like as long as anyone verifying the signed results asks SPIRE for the trust bundle it should expect to be used, im still not seeing how having access to the cert is required

The authority creates a bunch of short-lived certs (and their key pairs). The signatures are generated from these short lived key pairs. The cert is the only thing that is linking the verification of the key used to sign to the authority (trust bundle). 

Trust Bundle: Verification authority (CA)
Cert: This key-pair  K belongs to pod X, and this information is endorsed by the verification authority
Signature: This content was produced by keypair K

So the signatures links the content to the keypair, but the certificate is required to link the keypair to the authority.


> probably a nit but: the cert/trust bundle would be for the entire taskrun, not for a particular step in the taskrun, is that right?

The way we have it laid out now, it does both:

Both will use same Trust Bundle

Signed TaskRun status:  protect against the task run tampering.
- Cert belongs to TektonController

Signed Result: protect against pod status termination message tampering. 
- Cert belongs to individual pods executing steps

comments.author: lbernick
comments.body:
It feels a bit strange to have code in `reconciler/taskrun` validating that matrix params aren't array params-- ideally the taskrun reconciler shouldn't have knowledge of matrix at all. could this validation be done at the pipelinerun level, and treat the matrix params as normal params by the time they get to the taskrun level? Or is it necessary to ensure that params passed via the matrix aren't declared as array params in the task?

My mental model of how this would work (based on tep 90) is that the params are declared as arrays in the pipeline, passed as matrix params in the pipeline task, and then passed from the pipeline task to the taskrun as a list of string params. If the params were declared as array params in the task, the taskrun reconciler would recognize that the string param passed didn't match the array param declared, and fail.

comments.author: lbernick

And we hope to extend it to `Pipelines` as well in the future after implementing `Pipelines` in `Pipelines`. Some of the logic that applies to `Tasks` is not applied to `Custom Tasks` to allow users to customize the functionality of their own reconcilers. If we want to change whether this validation should be skipped for `Custom Tasks`, we could address it separately for all `Parameters` (in both `params` and `matrix` fields) as opposed to this PR that's focused on `matrix` only. What do you think?

> Rather than pass in matrix params separately, any reason to not just include them in the existing slice of params to validate?

@lbernick - The existing slice of params is checking if the type of params provided in the pipeline matches the type of params in taskspec (string to string, and array to array). However, we want the type of params provided in the matrix to be array and the type of params they are substituting in the taskspec to be string. Because the types do not match for matrix params, we can't pass it to the existing validation and that's why we have its own validation. Does that clarify?

We [landed](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/blob/main/teps/0090-matrix.md#combinations-of-parameters-in-the-matrix) on providing the matrix only initially in line with providing the "minimal  information needed" as proposed in TEP-0100. The Combinations type with MatrixID and Parameters sets us up for this possible extension to align with the Kubernetes API convention of [subobjects over maps](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md#lists-of-named-subobjects-preferred-over-maps). If we find that users don't need the complete information, we can switch to maps only given that it's only an implementation detail now.

comments.body:
sorry to keep pushing on this-- this reads more like a docstring for `isCancelled` which makes me wonder if there is some overlap between those two functions?

To clarify, when the pipelinerun is in stopping mode, for a non-matrixed taskrun it will only schedule it if it's cancelled/failed and has remaining retries. For a matrixed taskrun, it will schedule a taskrun if it is cancelled or failed with remaining retries **only if all other matrixed taskruns are done** (which includes being cancelled)?

If any matrixed taskrun is cancelled, does that mean all the others will be cancelled? It seems to me like we should be scheduling a matrixed taskrun in stopping mode if it's cancelled/failed with remaining retries, regardless of the state of the other matrixed taskruns.

comments.author: jerop
comments.body:
You were right, switched it to using `t.isCancelled()` instead of repeating the same logic.

The docstring wasn't reflecting what was happening, even for non-matrixed cases.  This function returns a list of pipelinetasks which should be executed next when the pipelinerun is stopping i.e. a list of failed pipelinetasks from candidateTasks which haven't exhausted their retries. If a pipelinetask is cancelled, the retries are not exhausted - they are not retryable.

For matrixed cases, isCancelled returns true if any run is cancelled and all other runs are done. Cancelling one taskrun from a matrix doesn't cancel the others, just the same way that one failing doesn't fail the others.

Sure, Here we are actually proposing two ways of generating the indices. One is just provide a number counter in the loop, so the task will take that number to do some actions. This is useful for handling big array file that cannot be passed via `results` due to the result size limit is 4KB.

comments.author: imjasonh
comments.body:
Hey sorry for missing this thread.

> @imjasonh to clarify, are you against dynamic generation of TaskRuns or against dynamic generation of Tasks themselves?

I think it's a tricky distinction. I'd like to prevent the case where a TaskRun can generate infinite subsequent TaskRuns, but even there there's a distinction: if a TaskRun generates N outputs that each feed into a TaskRun, and that N is bounded (either explicitly by some limit we impose, or just implicitly because you have to count to N before proceeding), I think it could be okay.

If a TaskRun is dynamically emitting results that are producing new TaskRuns _as results are emitted_, you can get into a situation where it's impossible to tell whether the feed will ever end, because you don't know whether the emitting end will ever stop. That's the more important one to avoid.

(I _think_ we're discussing the former scenario, which I think could be fine. Please let me know if I'm misunderstanding.)

comments.body:
A few potential requirements that we could include (if possible i think it would be really useful to express the requirements in terms such that a) we only mention design choices such as cosign in the proposal and b) we can be as clear as possible about what 'trusted' and 'safe' mean in this context:

* There is a process by which a Task or Pipeline can be marked as "trusted" (haha I'm not defining trusted BUT what I'm trying to say is that trust = owners of the Task or Pipeline explicitly sign off on the contents in some way)
* Verification can ensure the contents of the Task or Pipeline have not been modified since being marked as "trusted"
* It is not possible to modify the Task or Pipeline in such a way that it has been modified and the verification will still pass (i.e. the Task or Pipelines does not contain the means of verification)
* Verification can be performed by Tekton Pipelines; Tekton Chains can see whether or not the verification occurred and know that it was signed off on by Tekton Pipelines (this might be a bit too far into the implementation - however im a bit worried that relying on annotations might not work here - i.e. i think we need to know the annotation wasn't just added by someone with permission to edit the TaskRun/PipelineRun)

yup, chains operate over taskRun results and a pipelineRun will cause taskRuns to be specified.

The taskRun either part of a pipeline or not triggers chains if it produces `IMAGES` as task result (or have image pipeline resource as an output). The high level goal here is to design the solution which can be extended to a pipeline and also complements [TEP-0084](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/blob/main/teps/0084-endtoend-provenance-collection.md). comments.author: priyawadhwa
comments.body:
@bobcatfish yah so the annotations could be edited to say pretty much anything. If you want to prevent that then this is where spire could come in -- with spire, the pipelines controller could add some annotation and also a signature over that annotation, which chains could then verify. you can configure spire to only sign requests that come from the tekton controller, so something else running the cluster wouldn't be able to do it.

to follow the current chains format for signing you would have the user specify a path to a private key (this could be in a k8s secret or in kms). you'd just have to make sure that nothing else in the cluster could sign with it!

:+1: thanks for adding the clarifying detail about the location of the verification logic.

I'm going to add an additional Risk to TEP-0060 somewhat related to this: since `ResourceRequest` objects are just CRDs they suffer the same problems as Tekton's other CRDs - they can be modified pretty much any time by someone with the right permissions. So conceivably a Task that's verified by a Resolver might not be the same Task that a TaskRun reconciler receives, since someone with access to the cluster and write-access to ResourceRequests could modify the content moments after resolution + verification completes. It's a different threat model than the one this TEP is addressing but I want to document that Risk somewhere.

Edit: added [the risk and possible mitigations](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/pull/547/files#diff-5aec90b863359ee289524e8d80aa7c9b22f80d796b22e740691105de994b606fR426).

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
s/s KMS doesn't work quite the same way as cosign since it's trying to minimize deps - you need to import all of the desired providers from https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore/tree/main/pkg/signature/kms manually, which will call [ProviderInit](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/sigstore/sigstore/pkg/signature/kms#ProviderInit) to register the prefix.

The reason for this is that the providers are a big source of the massive dependency creep in cosign and related tools, since the cloud providers will pull in their corresponding SDKs.

I don't think we want to put this dependency burden on pipelines - at the very least you should make this its own module, though you may find it easier to just break this out into its own repo in the tektoncd org.

comments.author: Yongxuanzhang
comments.body:
I have updated the api, and verify logic to make it similar to policy-controller.
To summarize:

1. We first fetch all VerificationPolices, then loop each policy to see if 1 of the patterns could match the resource's source. If so adds the Policy to `matchedPolicies`. If no VerificationPolices is found in the namespace we will try to fetch keys from configmap. If no matchedPolicies we will fail the verification.
2. For all matchedPolicies we need to make sure the resource can pass all of them. To pass one policy the resource has to pass at least 1 authority.

So for policies level we will have a "AND" logic, and for authorities level we will have "OR" logic. This is the same as sigstore's logic.

comments.body:
hm im thinking it might be simpler to just fail in this case

a few factors to consider:
* input validation and trust boundaries: to some extent it makes sense to assume that input has been sanitized at some known level so you don't need to keep chekcing it repeatedly; so for us we should to some extent be able to assume that validation has happened on inputs HOWEVER asometimes that isn't the case e.g. through a bug - but you need to weigh the cost of constantly checking inputs and duplicating logic against the risk; TL;DR as much as possible have one place in the code where validation is supposed to happen so you can make assumptions about the quality of data provided to other functions and not repeat the check repeatedly
* BUT what if a function can't work correctly without certain data? e.g. in this case a verifier can't be constructed correctly unless the key is provided - i would treat this as an error, i.e. not duplicating input validation but simply failing b/c the function cant do it's job
* As much as possible, functions should be self contained and shouldn't need to be aware of how they are called - in this case, this test case seems to be saying 'we can let this go because we know some other function later is taking care of this for us' - but what if that changes? making assumptions like this couples the two functions together and the order they are called in

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
+1 to what Lee said - having to pass in 2 status objects, one of which we expect to be nil feels like an awkward interface to use. (I'm also concerned we need to pass in 10+ parameters to this func - it would probably be worth look into refactoring this into a dedicated client in another PR, since a majority of these values are just passed through from the receiver).

I'd lean towards the alternative you mentioned of returning some sort of signal and handling it as needed here. IIUC the 4 cases we're interested in are:

1. Returned successfully
2. Returned successfully with warning
3. Failed because of validation
4. Failed because of something else

1 and 4 are pretty straight forward. For 3, I think you could do this by implementing a `VerificationError` type and checking for it here.

2 is the trickiest, because depending on how you interpret it it may or may not be an "error". I think this is a case where it might make sense to return an error but still hold value in the other return values depending on what happened. I see a few options:
- Return resource + `VerificationError`, let the caller determine warning state (this might be tricky if you need to query the policies though).
- Add something to `VerificationError` that let's you encode the warning state (or create a new error type).
- Wrap the response with something that would let you pass back a non-error warning.

I'm fine with any of these options - your choice! (also open to other ideas).

comments.author: Yongxuanzhang
comments.body:
Discussed with @lbernick offline, to summarize I think this is a good point but I don't think it will happen. 
Though remote resolution seems async, but it is achieved by returning ErrRequestInProgress, https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/163ec59f2ccb05dc0aa804de40ac5eb85cd3c7ce/pkg/reconciler/taskrun/taskrun.go#L330-L333 so taskrun will continue to next reconcile loop until we fetch the task. 

But trusted resources verification is currently bundled with remote resolution, the verification will only happen when remote resolution is successful. So in multiple reconcile loops, the remote resolution and verification will be called together in one loop.  And `storeTaskSpecAndMergeMeta` will be called only when remote resolution is done and we return the VerificationResult

Another case is that, for the following loops after the remote resolution and verification, since we execute `storeTaskSpecAndMergeMeta`, GetTaskFuncFromTaskRun will return a taskspec and nil VerificationResult, but this is expected since we don't need to verify it if it has been verified before.

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
Something to balance when thinking about webhook vs reconcile validation - validation before admission is the safer strategy because the resource can be blocked before downstream informers are aware of them.

Other OCI based policy webhooks (OPA, Kyverno, sigstore/policy-controller) seem to do fine with network based lookups at admission time, though I get we also want to dedup fetching efforts between this and RemoteResolution.

If we go down the reconcile validation path, we should be careful about documenting when resources are considered trusted and how that information is exposed to users in the Run status (e.g. it might be worth having a dedicated termination status marking a Run as unverified?). Even then, there may still be some utility in a webhook based validation to make sure that the Run object itself hasn't been tampered with. 🤔

Resources (`Task`, `Pipeline`) will be verified *both* when applied to the cluster *and* when referenced in `taskRun`/`pipelineRun`. public-key-paths:

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
I think this is probably more trouble than it's worth.

In order for this to work, client versions need to stay in sync with the server (and potentially also other server-side configuration like the alpha feature flag). Any time either of these change, you risk breaking the signatures which would be a backwards incompatible change, which can also have rippling effects for the catalog, etc.

If we're skipping the mutating webhook, this already means that we're not modifying the object from what the user already gave us - instead of requiring a replay of the defaulting behavior we can just validate the message as the user gave it to us, and handling the defaulting at reconcile.

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
A caveat to this is skipping the mutating webhook would technically be a backwards incompatible change since it alters the response back to clients (though I highly doubt users are relying on its behavior - AFAICT it only sets param/result types).

Fine while it's opt-in, but if we do want to make the 2 paths consistent (which I'm in favor of) we should plan to start those deprecation timers ASAP.

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
My guess is this will probably be wanted sooner rather than later, since it's much easier for maintenance to have both paths have the same logic rather than have to have different assumptions depending on whether the mutating webhook ran or not.

To support verification you're already going to make sure similar defaulting behavior happens in the reconciler anyway, and there shouldn't be a harm in doing this post-mutating webhook for non-verified objects since they should produce the same result. If defaulting is happening at reconcile for all requests and we're allowing certain requests (i.e. verified resources) to skip the mutating webhook, then the mutating webhook isn't adding value and can just be removed since even non-verified resources should be able to safely skip the webhook as well.

This doesn't change this design, just more-so an FYI to other projects that this will be happening since this will change the stored API object for created objects which may be considered a backwards incompatible change - though I suspect most other tools are agnostic to the defaulting that the webhook is doing and won't even notice it's gone. If we need to follow the deprecation policy strictly here I'd rather do it sooner than later, since the main reason I can see keeping the webhook around is for backwards-compatibility (and may eventually be a blocker for removing the feature flag).

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
I don't think this is a good idea to support globally, though I get why we'd want something like this for incremental adoption. It would be generally be bad if Tasks could circumvent verification just by renaming to something that's not covered by policy, and new Tasks that are probably riskier would be exempted by default since they're unlikely to match existing policies.

Instead of making verification opt-in, it would probably be safer to make the mode opt-out on a per-policy basis (see [`ClusterImagePolicySpec.mode`](https://github.com/sigstore/policy-controller/blob/main/docs/api-types/index.md#clusterimagepolicyspec) for an example). This way things are directed to the more secure way by default, forcing users to either configure the matching policy or explicitly opt out the Tasks.

comments.body:
Happy to defer code comments for implementation PRs, but I don't think there's a need for a failure condition - I think this should this be represented as ConditionVerification with a failure status.

IIUC:
- condition = what were you checking (did this succeed? is this ready? Did this verify?)
- status = what is the value of the condition? (Usually True/false)
- reason = why did this happen? (Generally stable enum value, i.e. similar to HTTP status codes - permission denied, not found, unauthorized, etc)
- message = why did this happen (human friendly message)

Also worth noting you don't _need_ reason/message if they don't provide additional value.

I think we should include init and pull time in the pre-start timeout.

If I have a task where step N specifies an image that I don't have access to (or I've typoed and the image doesn't exist), then that container won't start and will go into `ImagePullBackOff`. _Apparently_ (I didn't know this until I tested it), step 0 will not proceed during this state. I don't know if this was intentional:

```
$ k get tr test-6j3k2
...
status:
  steps:
  - container: step-unnamed-0
    imageID: docker.io/library/ubuntu@sha256:626ffe58f6e7566e00254b638eb7e0f3b11d4da9675088f4781a50ae288f3322
    name: unnamed-0
    running:
      startedAt: "2021-10-25T14:26:02Z"
  - container: step-unnamed-1
    name: unnamed-1
    waiting:
      message: Back-off pulling image "non-existent"
      reason: ImagePullBackOff
```

(step 0 has started, but hasn't produced any logs indicating execution has actually started).

If that's the case, I'd rather have this task time out under the (presumably shorter) pre-start timeout regime than have it wait and get timed out by the longer task timeout.

comments.author: pritidesai
comments.body:
The use cases for this feature request were listed as:

* The user has N number of `pipelineTasks` running in parallel. This is very resource intensive and causing a huge load on a node. This load is causing other unrelated `taskRuns` (independent or part of a pipeline) to timeout without getting executed. How to save those unrelated `taskRuns` from timing out?

* Create extreme high number of `pipelineRuns` and `taskRuns` resulting in an overloaded cluster. These `pipelineRuns` could be a million runs of the same `pipeline` or  a combination of N different `pipelines`. These `pipelines` could be related or unrelated i.e. accessing the same remote resources. When a `node` is overloaded with such `fire and forget` nature of the operation, the expectation is to somehow maintain a `queue` of such `pipelineRuns`/`taskRuns` and cancel them when a new `pipelineRuns` are created. The pipeline controller has all the freedom to cancel any `pipelineRuns` from the `queue`.

* Align with GCP [queueTtl](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/build-config-file-schema#queuettl)

comments.author: bobcatfish
comments.body:
I have a few thoughts about this:
1. Instead of using map[string] I suggest we take the same approach as [taskRunSpecs](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/main/docs/pipelineruns.md#specifying-taskrunspecs) in PipelineRuns which serve a very similar function - and this is also a [kubernetes api design convention](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md#lists-of-named-subobjects-preferred-over-maps)
2. Even with the above change I have mixed feelings about being able to specify this per step and introducing the `*` syntax.

Re. (1)

We'd end up with something more like:

```yaml
spec:
  taskRef:
    name: image-build-task
  stepResources:
  - stepName: my-step
     requests:
       memory: 1Gi
```

Re. (2)

The `*` syntax also gives me pause b/c afaik we don't have a syntax like that anywhere else in our API - except in the context of array params https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/main/docs/tasks.md#substituting-array-parameters which are (slowly) adopting a JSONPath syntax. The `*` in this context isn't part of something like JSON and also implies that we might start putting other logic into this field (e.g. what if you wanted to use a regex here) which I feel is a can of worms I'd rather avoid.

One possible way around this, if we change this to a named subobject is that we could have a field to indicate that an entry should apply to all steps (vs. overloading the name), e.g. something like:

```yaml
spec:
  taskRef:
    name: image-build-task
  stepResources:
  -  applyTo: allSteps
     requests:
       memory: 1Gi
```

If we pursue a syntax like that, we have a few options, e.g. we could have an `applyTo` which completely replaces the stepname (effectively the same as the proposed idea to overload teh name field but a bit more explicit)

We could also use this field to allow step and sidecar specific overrides without needing to give them their own top level sections, e.g.:

```yaml
spec:
  taskRef:
    name: image-build-task
  stepResources:
  -  applyTo: allSteps/allSidecars
      requests:
        memory: 1Gi
```

Something like this approach could give us more flexibility later (e.g. if users wanted to apply these constraints to ALL containers, even the tekton generated containers)

Great point, I think this was an oversight on my part that we haven't made any communications yet on these feature flags. I wasn't thinking of this as a "deprecation" since the features are still around.

As for stabilizing OCI bundles, @sbwsg can you weigh in here? It sounds like they won't have to change much for remote resolution. I don't have a good sense on how well they are working right now.

We serialize the `Finally` section of a `v1beta1` Pipeline into an annotation if a client requests the `v1alpha1` version. When a client submits a `v1alpha1` version of a Pipeline with that annotation present the process reverses and the `v1beta1` object is recreated with the `Finally` section in-tact: https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/7a0a988cafaa64ff3e08969fa66f8521638d9b52/pkg/apis/pipeline/v1alpha1/pipeline_conversion.go#L142-L177

We don't do this for any other `v1beta1`-only fields. So, for example, when a `v1alpha1` client requests a `v1beta1` Pipeline with When Expressions, we simply drop them on the floor. If that client then re-applies the `v1alpha1` version the stored `v1beta1` version will be updated and the `when` expressions will be gone.

For a while we were [working on an approach](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/pull/3854) where we take the entire `v1beta1` object and serialize it into an annotation when clients request `v1alpha1`, but it proved to be a complex and imperfect workaround.

My immediate priority with Tekton Resolution is some level of git support, and I'm going to be out of office starting in early April through August/September. I'll try to get a bundles resolver written up before I leave but I can't make any promises at all around that, sorry. I don't expect it's a lot of effort to get it working but in terms of stability I'm not the right person to take that on until third or fourth quarter of this year.

In terms of bringing OCI Bundles into `stable` in Pipelines - it's up to the maintainers of Pipelines to decide how they want that to work: decide to bring [Bundles into `beta` in Tekton Pipelines](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/issues/3661), wait on Resolution to implement and graduate it, or ... something else?

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
I'm not sure I fully I agree on the documentation part. 
I think that when we release the `v1` version of a CRD, all fields of that CRD should be properly documented.
We can start producing the `v1` version of the CRD, but the moment we add in the release notes that `v1` is our primary CRD version it should be documented.
Other project `v1` documentation issues are not in scope for the CRD `v1`.

comments.author: lbernick
comments.body: That's a great point! I'll make those changes.

comments.author: vdemeester
comments.body:
I would add something here: v1 for Tekton Pipelines doesn't really make sense to me, it's very similar to v1 for the Tekton project as a whole really, only on the Pipeline component. 
This TEP is solely about publishing `v1` API on tektoncd/pipeline component. The "release" version of tektoncd/pipeline (aka the software version / git tag / …) doesn't need to be `v1` (and probably shouldn't be even).
As an example, knative publish v1 of the API and a 1.0.0 release at different time (I don't remember which one came first though 😛 )

comments.author: lbernick
comments.body:
I definitely agree about decoupling the software v1 release with the v1 api release (that was the intention of this PR 😅 ). My thought process was:
- some stuff in this TEP doesn't really make sense to block the release of v1 versions of our crds
- but it's still things we would consider useful to be a production-ready (sort of a v1 product)
- rather than eliminate the goals for metrics/performance/better docs, maybe we just clarify the scope of this TEP and state that we can release a v1 version of the CRDs whenever we want

Do you think it would be better to change the TEP title, or to descope anything that's not strictly related to api versioning?

FWIW I do think the concept of a v1 version of Pipelines does have some meaning-- we want Pipelines as a project to be usable given the crds and docs that we have-- but it could make sense to make this TEP scoped to just API versioning. I would want to keep the thoughts around production readiness *somewhere* though.

comments.author: vdemeester
comments.body:
> Do you think it would be better to change the TEP title, or to descope anything that's not strictly related to api versioning?

Not necessarily. Some things might not be directly be "API" but we could/would want them to be tackled before we "publish" a `v1` API. (I don't see too many out of the bat but still)

> FWIW I do think the concept of a v1 version of Pipelines does have some meaning-- we want Pipelines as a project to be usable given the crds and docs that we have-- but it could make sense to make this TEP scoped to just API versioning. I would want to keep the thoughts around production readiness somewhere though.

We should definitely aim to create a `v1.0.0` release of pipeline (meaning, a `v1.0.0` on `tektoncd/pipeline`) but it is decoupled from "the project publishing and supporting the `v1` API types".

On production readiness, given that it is already used relately widely in "production" by quite some users/customers, we may want to define what we mean by that 🙃. The "pipeline" component is stable and kind-of already ready for production (as production is most likely a CI system.. which is less critical than other type of "service"). But "pipeline" is not a platform though, it's just a "component of a framework for creating CI/CD systems" (as state on tekton.dev 👼🏼). But that's probably another topic 😝

comments.author: lbernick
comments.body: OK-- I think it might be good to rename this TEP to "pipelines v1" to reflect that some of its contents are not about the API. I also agree on avoiding/clarifying the term "production ready" 😅 but I'm not sure how best to word this instead... I agree that versioning for tekton as a whole is probably out of scope. Any other changes you'd like to see here?

You can just say we will start serving v1 versions, and then one release later, we will swap the stored version to v1, mark v1beta1 as deprecated, and document that the EOL for v1beta1 is 9 months after that release.

Describing the code PR in this TEP is a bit too much implementation detail IMO.

comments.author: lbernick
comments.body:
This is a good question, I've been thinking we should be more explicit about defining this. The use cases I've identified so far for extensibility are:

- Different VCS providers: e.g. google could support [cloud source repositories](https://cloud.google.com/source-repositories/docs), and there are plenty of other alternatives to GitHub
- Different ways of connecting to the VCS providers we do support: e.g. if a platform builder wants to introduce additional steps for a user connecting their GitHub account. For example, connecting a repo using a platform builder's github app, or introducing a step to link a GitHub repo to a user's account (this idea is admittedly not fully fleshed out but I think @alhuizenga may be thinking about CUJs related to repo connections)
- Easier ways to send notifications to external systems, e.g. designing a mechanism for building slack notification support that doesn't involve sending slack notifications as part of your CI pipeline
- Storing secrets somewhere other than k8s secrets, such as hashicorp vault or google/aws secrets managers. This could potentially be built into pipelines, or maybe these platform builders should just be responsible for implementing CSI secrets store drivers as hashicorp vault has done.
- Storing pipeline data somewhere other than PVCs, like AWS S3. Another idea that we're already exploring building directly into pipelines.

Curious to hear which of these use cases you think are the most important. I'm not sure exactly what you mean about swapping implementation but that isn't a use case I had in mind.

comments.author: lbernick
comments.body:
Great point! The only docs I'm aware of for Tekton conformance are this [api spec](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/main/docs/api-spec.md) and specifically this [section on params](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/main/docs/api-spec.md#param); however, it only details which api fields must be supported and not which param syntax tekton implementations are required to support. This would be a really useful thing to have as part of our API spec. FYI @XinruZhang since Xinru is working on a more up to date conformance spec.

I do think `$(tt.params.foo)` syntax is more in line with Pipelines param syntax than `{{ foo }}`. Would it be possible to replace `{{ foo }}` with something more Tekton-esque, like `$(context.event.repo_url)` or something like that?

comments.author: lbernick

With workflows, we clearly want to make it much easier for a user to trigger pipelineruns based on events from a connected repo. However, I'm not yet sure if we want to tackle the goals of automatically keeping configuration stored in a repo in sync with the cluster, and running configuration included in opened PRs. WDYT?

comments.author: XinruZhang
comments.body:
Thanks for having me in the conversation! @lbernick!

Re @chmouel

> Is Tekton triggers conformant to Tekton pipeline?

Great question!! Not for now and unknown for the future (likely not for the near future).

The conformance policy will be initially defined for Tekton Pipeline service which takes stable Pipelines CRDs in, schedules and runs the workloads defined by those CRDs. Any vendor that wants to provide Tekton Pipeline Service needs to conform to the policy that's defined for those stable CRDs.

The plan is for the first step, we'd like to start with four Tekton primitives: Task, TaskRun, Pipeline and PipelineRun which have been promoted to V1.

Therefore, for triggers, it is not part of **Tekton Pipeline Service**, and it produces Tekton Pipelines primitives (Task, TaskRuns, Pipeline, PipelineRuns) that will be taken by **Tekton Pipelines Service**, so it would be fine for Triggers to use different variable expansion syntax as long as the Pippelines primitives it produces conform to the conformance policy we define for **Tekton Pipelines Service**.

Yes the `$(tt.params.variable)` syntax can be tedious, but I wouldn't think that's a problem. Workflow is actually the very right project to ease the tedious. I would love to take quote a metaphor from @bobcatfish about the Tekton Pipelines:

Tekton Pipelines is more of plumbing instead of toilet – The Tekton Pipelines is more of an underline infrastructure, let other works to improve the UX.  For instance – Triggers, catalog etc.

> Tekton pipelines don't necessarily understand the $(tt.params.variable) syntax better than a {{ variable }} syntax?

Yeah it doesn't necessarily if we are designing it in the first place, but now we've heavily relied on the syntax, both developers and users are already familiar with it.

cc @dibyom 

In the future, we may also expand the conformance policy:
- include not only primitives for Tekton Pipelines Services, but also for Triggers.
- include APIs that reach mature state, for example, Custom Task, once it is promoted to V1, we may also want to include it in the Conformance policy: https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/issues/5700.

comments.author: dibyom
comments.body:
> Is Tekton triggers conformant to Tekton pipeline? because Tekton pipelines doesn't necessary understand better the $(tt.params.variable) syntax more than a {{ variable }} syntax?

The difference is that in Triggers, you use the $(tt.params) syntax in a TriggerTemplate that does understand that syntax. While in PAC, you are using {{ variable }} in a PipelineRun object which does not understand it. IMO calling it a pipelinerun when it contains syntax not supported in a regular pipelinerun is a bit confusing.

I can try again later, and almost certainly will, but I think that if the messiness of these functions ends up as the last thing holding this PR up, this may be a case where we need to plug our nose and accept the smell.

comments.author: abayer
comments.body:
and fwiw, the messiness feels to me to largely be down to the fact that `pr.Status.TaskRuns` and `pr.Status.Runs` are maps, while `pr.Status.ChildReferences` is an array. So while updating `pr.Status.TaskRuns` and `pr.Status.Runs` is just a matter of "oh, this key isn't there yet? Let's add it! Oh, it is? Then update its value!" without having to worry about anything else already in the map, updating `pr.Status.ChildReferences` means we need to make sure that everything already in the array is still in the array when we're done, and we have to make changes to the elements in the array at different points in the process. That's why I added the `childRefByPipelineTask` temporary map - so we can keep all the existing references, add new ones, and make changes to references without needing to do "ok, iterate over `pr.Status.ChildReferences` until we find one with the right `PipelineTaskName`, now make changes to it, etc".

That last bit would admittedly be simpler if `pr.Status.ChildReferences` was a `[]*ChildStatusReference` rather than a `[]ChildStatusReference` as it is now, but it'd still be a mess.

It's definitely better from a Kubernetes API perspective to have an array instead of a map, but the downside is that updating individual elements in an array is always going to be uglier than updating individual elements in a map.

comments.author: abayer
comments.body:
Ok, I got hooked on trying to figure out a less messy way and am maybe making some progress, but I forgot another thing that makes it more complicated (besides what I mentioned in https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/pull/4706#discussion_r839942364) - we have to generate the `TaskRun`/`Run` name for new ones, and if we're handling updating `TaskRuns`/`Runs` separately from updating `ChildReferences`, then when we've got `embedded-status='both'`, we need to make sure that we only generate a new name once. So, with `ChildReferences` as our first choice for source of truth, when we go to update `TaskRuns` after updating `ChildReferences`, we have to use the new `TaskRun` name we generated when updating `ChildReferences` again in `TaskRuns`.

I've made real progress in significantly simplifying the condition check handling part, so if I can nail the right way to do the `TaskRun` name generation once-and-only-once, I may be able to refactor this. It'll still be fairly ugly and have a good amount of duplicated code, but I think the current mess is the only way to avoid the duplicated code.

comments.author: abayer
comments.body: (specifically, that's names for condition check `TaskRun`s, not all `TaskRun`s. Boy is this all confusing logic...)

comments.author: abayer
comments.body: @lbernick Ok! I think I may have a better approach - see https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/pull/4706/commits/18521d4dd6e5802d56e6687bcc8ad4c2b6071ac0. It's not perfect yet - needs some cleanup/comments/test changes (specifically tests for the new `updatePipelineRunStatusFromSlices`, `getNewConditionChecksForTaskRun`,  and `updatePipelineRunStatusFromChildRefs`, a test for `updatePipelineRunStatusFromRuns`, and changes to the test for `updatePipelineRunStatusFromTaskRuns`), but it does decouple and simplify things. I'd love your thoughts!

comments.author: pritidesai
comments.body:
pipelineRun status contains `startTime`, `completionTime`, `conditions` (indicating success or failure of pipelineRun itself), `pipelineResults`, `pipelineSpec`,  a map of `taskRuns`, and a map of `runs`.

Here, we are trying to optimize the map of `taskRun` and `run`. Each `taskRun` and `run` in turn contains `startTime`, `completionTime`, `conditions` (indicating success or failure of taskRun/run itself), `podName`, a list of steps, `taskResults`, and `taskSpec`.

```go
type ResourceStatus struct {
```

```yaml
status:
    completionTime: "2020-05-04T02:19:14Z"
    conditions:
      - lastTransitionTime: "2020-05-04T02:19:14Z"
```

Opening another comment thread here since GitHub PRs don't allow reopening outdated comment threads. 😢  (original thread - https://github.com/tektoncd/community/pull/616#discussion_r796785042)

We had some additional discussion about this alternative that we were somewhat split on. Would love additional input here!

The rough idea is to reference the sub-resources with TypeMeta+ObjectMeta to be in line with [multiple resource reference recommendations](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md#multiple-resource-reference) and give us a way to handle arbitrary types (e.g. TaskRun, Run, PipelineRun(?)), but also a way for us to distinguish versions of the same resource (e.g. v1 vs v1beta1 Tasks) (related discussion in https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/issues/4543 for how we want to handle mixed apiVersion definitions). e.g.

```go
type ResourceStatus struct {
	runtime.TypeMeta
	metav1.ObjectMeta
	duckv1beta1.Status
}
```

Even though it's slightly more verbose, it gives us more flexibility in the types we can support now and in the future.

The main downside is by using the same message type, we're making it more difficult to add type-specific fields in the future (unless we use some sort of duck typing). However, since minimal statuses are intended to be ref-like objects anyway, it's unclear if we will actually need this.

Let us know what you think!

In fact the `PipelineRun` reconciler today, at the beginning of every reconcile cycle, scans existing `TaskRuns` to reconcile the `PipelineRun` status against what's available in the cluster. 

The reconciler, from that point on, only uses internal structures to deal with this local cache of `TaskRun` and `Run` status, which is finally written at the end of the reconcile in case of changes.

comments.author: afrittoli

For the [`ObjectMeta` ](https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/df993592a122931b8aac4db57689e09458a2332c/pkg/apis/meta/v1/types.go#L116) part, it sounds good, but it shouldn't be more than `Name` and perhaps `Namespace`. We don't support cross-namespace references today, not sure if we will add them. I would not replicated labels, annotations, ownerreferences etc as those are not needed to identify the resource uniquely, and storing them in the `PipelineRun` would again mean double updates, since labels and annotations can be inherited from `Tasks`. Considering how many labels and annotations we setup in native Tekton alone (between pipeline, triggers, results and chains), replicating them would also mean using a lot of extra space in etcd.

For the `duckv1beta1.Status` part, I would not include it, because it means again extra space, extra writes to the `PipelineRun` so extra reconcile cycles triggered - and I don't see the advantage for the controller of having that information locally in the `PipelineRun` resource.

The downside of this is that when adding something to the list, we need to check for uniqueness across the entire content of the list.

comments.author: dibyom
comments.body:
I think having a "both" option can be a very useful temporary option to ensure a seamless transition experience for Tekton API clients. The "both" approach is how we generally do backwards incompatible API changes to support older clients.

1. On release X, we have "both" as the default. CLI/Dashboard/any other clients have to rely on the old fields.

2. Operator updates pipeline to release X+1 where "minimal" is the default. CLI/Dashboard/any other clients are now all broken until they can be upgraded to a version that uses the new fields.

3. Because the only supported options are "full" and "minimal", operators have to ensure that every client is upgraded to a version that supports the new fields when they want to upgrade to version. 
One workaround for this would be for the clients to add in logic to support both the new and old fields at the same time but then by not adding the "both" option, we are essentially forcing our each of our clients to add the logic to support both versions.

4. If we did have a "both" option, the Tekton operator will flip the option to "both" for a short amount of time while allowing the clients to upgrade. Once all clients are upgraded, the operator will flip the switch to "minimal".

comments.author: lbernick
comments.body:
in the TEP i have the resources applied only to the first container, but I think it would actually be better to split them among the containers. The reason is that limitrange default requests are split among the containers. consider this example:

2 steps
task level memory: 1Gi
limitrange default requests: 600Mi

If you split the task level resources between containers you'll have each container with 500Mi (which is what we want). If you just apply them to one container, the limitrange defaults will kick in for the container without resources and you'll have one container with 1Gi and one with 300Mi (not what we want). 

I'll update the TEP to clarify this.

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
This looks good. We might want to prevent overriding of Tekton defined labels and annotations though.
For instance, in this example:

```yaml
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1beta1
kind: TaskRun
metadata:
  annotations:
    chains.tekton.dev/retries: "3"
    chains.tekton.dev/signed: failed.   
    pipeline.tekton.dev/affinity-assistant: affinity-assistant-24428a19af
    pipeline.tekton.dev/release: 6b5710c
    results.tekton.dev/record: default/results/5ffb52cc-ce6f-466b-8ddf-827b955cf6c5/records/43f5e888-b935-4264-91c2-7ff54fd09b3e
    results.tekton.dev/result: default/results/5ffb52cc-ce6f-466b-8ddf-827b955cf6c5
  labels:
    tekton.dev/memberOf: tasks
    tekton.dev/pipeline: catalog-publish
    tekton.dev/pipelineRun: publish-catalog-tekton-ghn4b
    tekton.dev/pipelineTask: git-clone
    tekton.dev/task: git-clone
    triggers.tekton.dev/eventlistener: tekton-cd
    triggers.tekton.dev/trigger: catalog
    triggers.tekton.dev/triggers-eventid: 5ffb52cc-ce6f-466b-8ddf-827b955cf6c5
```

- pipeline.tekton.dev annotations are set by the pipeline controller
- chains.tekton.dev annotations are set by chains
- results.tekton.dev annotations are set by results
- tekton.dev labels are set by the pipeline controller or coming from the catalog
- triggers.tekton.dev labels are set by triggers

```suggestion
With SLSA being established, there is a rise in demand for achieving richer provenance within attestations. [In-toto](https://github.com/in-toto/attestation) provides a way for supporting richer provenance inside Predicates. Tekton Chains currently supports multiple kinds of attestations and the in-toto attestation format is one of the popular ones in the open source community. Tekton Chains currently use [Results](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/main/docs/tasks.md#emitting-results) and [Params](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/main/docs/tasks.md#specifying-parameters) for such type of attestation generation. It uses type hinting for capturing a CI/CD pipeline's inputs and outputs’ provenance info in string formats. The concepts of `inputs` and `outputs` come from [SLSA provenence v0.2](https://slsa.dev/provenance/v0.2). As Chains is planning to support more complex provenance info and structures, the current string formatted type hinting will not accomodate the scalibilities and integretity it needs, as Pipeline didn’t provide structured provenance info generation in TaskRuns and we are capturing unstructured provenance info from TaskRuns in scattered ways. With [TEP 0075](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/blob/main/teps/0075-object-param-and-result-types.md) and [TEP 0076](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/blob/main/teps/0076-array-result-types.md), TaskRun can provide features of structured results and params.
```

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
```suggestion
Results is not an ideal place to have the provenance metadata populated for the artifacts, since Results are provided by Pipeline authors. When people are looking for provenance, the metadata being provided should ideally be trustful and unchangeable after generation. How can we guarantee the provenance metadata can be trusted? Assuming the Tekton Pipeline being installed and where the Runs are operated are trustful, one missing piece to comply to SLSA level L3 is that the Run yaml being submitted is a trustful config, which can be fulfilled by [TEP 091: Trusted Resource](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/pull/739). The other missing piece is that we want to make sure the generated provenance data shouldn't be changeable by any untrusted threads. TaskRun and PipelineRun `status` field satisfies these needs, as only Pipeline controller is able to generate info within this field. To extend the previous trustful setup, we can allow Trusted Tasks to modify the field as well: when Trusted Tasks are being used, Pipeline Controller can verify the Trusted Tasks being used in a Run, and let Trusted Tasks to generate provenance metadata a new field under `status` fields.
```

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body: I think the thing I like the most about not tying provenance to to results is that authors don't need to pre-declare provenance result data - a Task can simply output it without needing it to be explicitly declared in a param. This makes it easier to work with when there's a variable amount of items that will be generated, though at the cost of making it hard to be consumed by other steps (though it's unclear to me whether there's a strong requirement for this at the moment).

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
I prefer this over requiring task authors to plumb through result names, though a few caveats:

Putting data in object keys means that we're breaking from the intoto spec - e.g. what happens if a user just outputs a vanilla intoto material? Is intoto compatibility a goal for this proposal (it feels like this is what we're aiming for, but it's not explicitly called out as a goal)?

By putting the field in the result spec, this has the nice property of not having to need to modify the payload the Task needs to output (e.g. it can be a vanilla intoto spec), but if we'll need a spec change it might make more sense to just move forward with the status-based provenance.

That said, maybe keeping the results to follow naming type hinting may still be the temporary pattern we should follow before the status-based provenance being landed. WDYT @wlynch @afrittoli ?

This verification would be hard to do in Chains, and having Task authors to do such verifications seems beneficial.

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
```suggestion
The in-toto provenance supports digest in terms of [DigestSets](https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/blob/main/spec/field_types.md#field-type-definitions) for an artifact, which means users can provide different digests for different digest SHAs. Since Pipeline Results cannot support nested objects yet, Chains is unable to support them at the moment. In the proposal, only one pair of SHA and digest can be provided. `DigestSets` can be supported when nested objects are supported in `Results`.
```

Rephrased - it's not that this is hard for Chains to support, it's that we're limited by what Pipelines supports.

> But how would we allow users to use Chains, if the string format type hinting is something we are looking to deprecate?

How confident are we in the status based provenance as the long term solution? It might make more sense to just move forward with that.
We could support a limited subset short term if needed (i.e. single, predefined artifacts) with the understanding that it's not a general purpose solution and can probably only be used in limited cases.
Since it sounds like we need Pipeline changes anyway to have a more general solution using params (i.e. object arrays), the difference between that and adding a new status field on the surface doesn't feel like that big of a delta.

comments.body: We have another use case not already covered here and not supported by workspaces (nor could they easily be) which is dynamic volumes. Sometimes, it is desired/opportune to create a volume (say backed by a configmap or secret) dynamically in a pipeline and then mount it into an already named volume mount in a task. This is not possible with workspaces because the workspace bindings need to be defined up front.

We could add a special page / section to document this feature as something we do not recommend to use unless in specific documented cases and specify security risks.

comments.author: lbernick
comments.body:
Thinking about this comment a bit more.. Giving good examples is a bit tricky. We don't want to write something that looks like you can actually use it, because we don't have any CustomRun controllers and we don't want users copy pasting the example and getting annoyed when it doesn't work. But at the same time I think the variable naming can "clue" ways we intend users to interact with this feature.

For example, here's a wait Task run (copied from experimental repo):
```
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Run
metadata:
  generateName: wait-run-
spec:
  ref:
    apiVersion: example.dev/v0
    kind: Wait
  params:
  - name: duration
    value: 10s
```
Maybe our example here could be:
```
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1beta1
kind: CustomRun
spec:
  ref:
    apiVersion: example.dev/v0
    kind: MyCustomKind
  params:
  - name: duration
    value: 10s
```
Here, I'd imagine the user wouldn't want to specify a "name" in the custom task ref, because it's more useful to define duration on the run. (Duration is more of a runtime feature than an authoring time feature.)

The `pipeline-loop` custom task has some examples where it is useful to specify a name in the custom task ref (e.g. https://github.com/tektoncd/experimental/blob/main/pipeline-loops/examples/simplepipelineloop.yaml) and could be adapted similarly.

WDYT? This might be something we can iterate on in the future.

comments.author: XinruZhang
comments.body:
@pritidesai 
> What does properly allude to here?

PiplineRun controller has hard code dependencies on status report of CustomRun controller: See [the code](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/38c739a5d0d9faff8c362462f8b6beee0458d978/pkg/reconciler/pipelinerun/resources/pipelinerunresolution.go#L258-L260), which [is used to decide if the CustomRun is failed or not](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/38c739a5d0d9faff8c362462f8b6beee0458d978/pkg/reconciler/pipelinerun/resources/pipelinerunresolution.go#L148).

@ScrapCodes 
> To ensure that cancellation is required, are we planning to have validations now or in future? if no, is this just a documentation change?

Yes I think we'll have code validations in the future in the ideal world. I opened an issue for it https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/issues/5700

> do we support pipeline level Timeout for custom task? I remember it was removed?

There are two kinds of timeout for Custom Task:
- One is [`PipelineTask.Timeout`](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/b15a80e5ab9299386024578ac25b1f42c4d364ac/pkg/apis/pipeline/v1beta1/pipeline_types.go#L229), which is passed to `CustomRunSpec.Timeout`.
- The other is [`PipelineRunSpec.Timeouts`](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/b15a80e5ab9299386024578ac25b1f42c4d364ac/pkg/apis/pipeline/v1beta1/pipelinerun_types.go#L247). 

What we removed is the first one. i.e. we stopped PipelineRun controller to modify CustomRun.status.Conditions upon CustomRun timeout -- (CustomRun executes more than `CustomRunSpec.Timeout`, see https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/pull/5658).

comments.body:
Hi @wlynch, thanks for your input and this is a good question 😀 . The short answer is **yes**. If artifacthub publishes 0.1, and I will  always be able to fetch 0.1.0

The artifact hub will always convert the [resource yaml version](https://github.com/tektoncd/catalog/blob/962f9005350b1acb359558b6c5aafc420e0beb46/task/git-clone/0.8/git-clone.yaml#L6) to semVer (i.e. `0.6` -> `0.6.0`) and the Hub uses the semVer to index the corresponding resource.
 
So technically you can publish a resource with yaml version `0.6` first (which is converted to `0.6.0` in the Hub), and then publish another yaml version of `0.6.0`, it just overrides the previous `0.6.0` version in the Hub. But the API will always return the latest `0.6.0`

The main reason I put such conversion is for backward compatibility, so that current users can keep version 0.6 in the resolver, and the type is default to `artifact`
