```yaml
  http: resolver-billy,resolver-b,resolver-a 
  oci: resolver-billy,resolver-c 
  git+https: resolver,billy,resolver-a
  *: resolver-billy
```

Above, for the specific formats where other resolvers are specifically subscribed to, we list `resolver-billy` as the first item since in your scenario, we want the request to go there first. To capture any other format not specified, we use the `*` key to indicate that `resolver-billy` has subscribed to all other schemes.

A few thoughts on `## Alternatives` which could be a section here. One alternative I can think of is => _Per-task `failFast` annotation_ which could look like this:

```yaml
tasks:
- name: critical-lint
  failFast: true    # if THIS fails, cancel everything
  taskRef:
    name: golangci-lint
- name: optional-coverage
  failFast: false   # if THIS fails, let others finish
  taskRef:
    name: coverage-report
```

This gives finer control. A lint failure stops everything immediately, but a coverage failure doesn't. The current proposal is all-or-nothing at the pipeline level which is fine but the TEP could explain why per-task granularity was not chosen (simplicity? can be added as a future enhancement?).

comments.author: afrittoli
comments.body:
Since the actual resources available on the node/nodepool where the workload gets scheduled are controlled by the platform admin, I thought this could be a global configuration.
I see that runtime users may need the ability to tune this as well, but I think it would be nice to have the ability to define some platform defaults, which could be overwritten by `Run` objects when needed.

Maybe it's too much, but I wonder if such profiles could be a CRD, then it would be possible to have a cluster scope profile or namespace-specific ones, to tune resource consumption in specific namespaces.
A CRD could even contain node selector rules to apply specific defaults depending on the node pool where the workload is scheduled.

comments.author: JordanGoasdoue
comments.body:
Thanks for the feedback. I agree a CRD-based design is the right way to go. It keeps v1 intact, gives platform admins clear control, and lets runs opt in when needed.

Here's the plan. We'll introduce a ComputeResourcesProfile CRD owned by platform admins. It defines sizes and scheduling via nodeAffinity. Then add an optional top-level spec.computeResourcesProfile on PipelineRun to select a profile by name, define one inline, or fetch via a resolver. No changes to taskRunSpecs.

On why nodeAffinity instead of nodeSelector, it's a superset that supports In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist, Gt, Lt, OR across terms, and soft preferences with preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution. A single field avoids precedence ambiguity and keeps the API small. If we want convenience later, we can accept nodeSelector as sugar and translate it to nodeAffinity internally.

Take this example ComputeResourcesProfile for non-GPU, CPU-intensive work.

```yaml
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1alpha1
kind: ComputeResourcesProfile
metadata:
  name: ci-high-cpu
spec:
  description: "CPU-intensive jobs (build/compile). Prefer compute-optimized, avoid spot."
  nodeAffinity:
    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: node.kubernetes.io/instance-type
          operator: In
          values: ["c5.large", "c5.xlarge", "c6i.large"]
        - key: eks.amazonaws.com/capacityType
          operator: NotIn
          values: ["SPOT"]
    preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
    - weight: 100
      preference:
        matchExpressions:
        - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          operator: In
          values: ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"]
  sizes:
    s:
      requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi" }
      limits:   { cpu: "1",    memory: "2Gi" }
    m:
      requests: { cpu: "1",    memory: "2Gi" }
      limits:   { cpu: "2",    memory: "4Gi" }
    l:
      requests: { cpu: "2",    memory: "4Gi" }
      limits:   { cpu: "4",    memory: "8Gi" }
```

And here's how it looks in a PipelineRun.

```yaml
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1
kind: PipelineRun
spec:
  pipelineRef:
    name: my-app-pipeline

  computeResourcesProfile:
    # Option A: reference a shared CRD by name
    name: ci-high-cpu

    # --- OR ---

    # Option B: define a one-off profile inline (same shape as CRD spec)
    # spec:
    #   nodeAffinity:
    #     requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
    #       nodeSelectorTerms:
    #       - matchExpressions:
    #         - key: node.kubernetes.io/instance-type
    #           operator: In
    #           values: ["t3.medium"]
    #   sizes:
    #     s:
    #       requests: { cpu: "100m", memory: "256Mi" }
    #       limits:   { cpu: "200m", memory: "512Mi" }

    # --- OR ---

    # Option C: fetch via resolver
    # ref:
    #   resolver: git
    #   params:
    #     - name: url
    #       value: https://github.com/my-team/tekton-profiles.git
    #     - name: revision
    #       value: main
    #     - name: pathInRepo
    #       value: profiles/ci-high-cpu.yaml
```

This TEP proposes a new field `runAfterAlways` for finally tasks that enables ordering between finally tasks **without breaking the guaranteed-execution contract**.

comments.author: aThorp96
comments.body: I think `step` should also be optional. That would allow controllers to add notices to a Run that are not specific to a step. For example the pipelinerun controller may add a warning notice to a pipelinerun if the pipeline doesn't have any tasks or if the pipelinerun uses a deprecated field like `spec.timeout`.

comments.author: aThorp96
comments.body:
I don't object to these fields, but they are more use-case specific for a system like PaC. Since the notices would be competing for space with results, it might be good to either omit them or develop a more terse syntax. It would be very easy for a linter job to blow up the storage with a large number of lint warnings. 

For example if there are 20 lint warnings on `some/very/long/path/to/a/deeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeply/nested/file/with/some/poor/formatting/that/has/to/fixed`, that's over 3.7kb of te 4kb termination message limit.

comments.author: aThorp96
comments.body: I think it would be good to include the usecase of controllers adding notices here.

Or at least we'll need to make sure this is handled gracefully/intuitively when a user mistakenly assumes `echo -n "some message" >> $(notices.path)` would be interpreted as `{"level": "info", "message": "some message"}`.

comments.author: aThorp96
comments.body:
```suggestion

#### Controller Author

As a *Tekton controller author*, I want a canonical way to reflect non-failure warnings and
information on runs which can be semantically consumed by other services, integrations, and users. 

```

comments.author: aThorp96
comments.body:
I think this is supposed to refer to the CR size limit, not CRD. 

It looks like the CR size limit defaults to 1.5M. We don't currently limit the number of results, and I've seen many a linter emit more than 100 warning lines. Does the limit here need to be a requirement or do you think it would suffice to either call out that a large number of notices may cause the CR to exceed the maximum size or restrict the size by `max-results-size`? 

Similarly, since a pipelinerun with many tasks may have a large number of notices, could we get away without bubbling the taskrun notices up to the pipelinerun? If the pipelinerun status states that the taskruns _have_ notices (maybe not even necessary) we could leave it up to controllers to get the notices from the taskruns directly. That would reduce duplication and for clusters with lots of pipelineruns with a lot of notices it may have a large difference in the etcd usage as well.

comments.author: aThorp96
comments.body:
I like the idea of the aggregation. I wonder if the CR size could be reduced by aggregating similarly to how we do with TaskRun statuses in the `Succeeded` condition:
```yaml
kind: PipelineRun
status:
  notices:
    - level: warning
      message: "task build emitted 2 warning notices"
    - level: warning
      message: "task lint emitted 12 warning notices"
    - level: info
      message: "task lint emitted 1 info notice"
```

This would increase the complexity of consuming the aggregated notices, since the client would have to fetch the TaskRun to get the actual notices, but that logic may already be necessary if a client wants to process notices which were truncated during aggregation.

Notices for the PipelineRun itself (like using deprecated fields) could still exist alongside these aggregation notices I think

comments.author: aThorp96
comments.body: Would this be achieved by setting the list type to `+listType=set` instead of `+listTyp=atomic`? Would it make sense to do this on the TaskRun as well?

comments.author: aThorp96
comments.body: Would this make sense to be a warning notice? 😁

comments.author: aThorp96
comments.body: When considering the size of the CR, I can see why this could be necessary. However I worry a limit like this would make the feature far less valuable in many use cases.

comments.author: aThorp96
comments.body:
For the intermediary RunResult schema, I would suggest we use a far smaller schema. As much as I hate the abbreviations, something like the below could make a difference when we're competing for bytes in the termination message. 
```go
type NoticeLevel string
const NoticeLevelWarning NoticeLevel = "w"
const NoticeLevelInfo NoticeLevel = "i"
type Notice struct {
    Level NoticeLevel `json:"l"`
    Message string `json:"m"`
    Step string `json:"s,omitempty"`
    File string `json:"p,omitempty"`
    StartLine *int `json:"sl,omitempty"`
    EndLine *int `json:"el,omitempty"`
}
```

A custom encoding format wouldn't be unwarranted in this domain either, IMO.

comments.author: aThorp96
comments.body:
This needs some clarification; I don't think this makes sense as a "priority model". Specifically:
- how to notices compare to artifacts and metadata (I assume they are lowest priority)
- Per-step cap and message length cap are necessary to document but I'm not sure they are part of the "priority model"

comments.author: aThorp96
comments.body: One alternative we haven't really discussed is storing these as Events instead of in the Run status. I haven't thought about this alternative too much, but I think it's worth considering the tradeoffs.

comments.author: vdemeester
comments.body: That's gonna be very tricky, as highlighted before termination message can be very small **and* varies depending on the number of containers (and in our case, steps).

comments.author: vdemeester
comments.body: Using sidecar-log is an issue as well, it's is not enabled by default, and it has shortcomings that makes it not scale that much.

comments.author: vdemeester
comments.body:
This makes the assumption that termination messages is 4KB is "stable", but it's not : https://github.com/tektoncd/pipeline/issues/4808, especially

> **The total size of termination messages of all containers in a pod cannot exceed 12 KB**. If the total size exceeds 12 KB, the state manager of Kubernetes sets a limit on the termination message sizes. **For example, if a pod contains four InitContainers and eight application containers, the state manager limits the termination message of each container to 1 KB**. This indicates that only the first 1 KB of the termination message of each container is intercepted.

comments.author: vdemeester
comments.body: I think https://github.com/tektoncd/community/pull/1248 might be more useful. Maybe those notices/warnings/.. could be just artifacts, and we could have a tool or a task (or the controllers) to make them pop up where we want them to be.

comments.author: vdemeester
comments.body:
One missing alternative is a set of re-usable step or task that could publish those to the right place (github, etc..) and be *injected* in tasks or pipeline (finally task).

Essentially, if we wanted to do what is proposed today without any changes, how would it look like in a Pipeline/Task ? What are the problems that comes with it (e.g. token required to publish to github, etc..) ?
